input: What is the process for deriving the replicator equation from a birth-death process?
expected_output: The replicator equation can be derived from a birth-death process in the limit of an infinite population, where the average payoff per game to an individual of type i in a population of composition x is given by the payoff matrix A and the fraction of individuals of type i. The derivation involves considering the birth and death rates of individuals of different types and taking the limit as the population size approaches infinity, resulting in the standard replicator equation given by dx_i/dt = x_i(π_i - π), where π_i is the average payoff to an individual of type i and π is the average payoff of the population.
context:
In this type of game one idea is dominant, and always has a higher payoff than the other type of idea. The replicator flow has constant sign; for the choice of payoff matrix in Fig. REF (b) it has an unstable fixed point at x=0, and a stable fixed point at x=1. The Sato-Crutchfield dynamics at \lambda >0 has an additional stable interior fixed point x^\star , which approaches unity as \lambda \rightarrow 0, see Fig. REF (a). In finite populations the dynamics is similar to that of the coexistence game when \lambda > 0. After an initial relaxation towards the interior fixed point, noise drives the system to fixation. Given that the fixed point is located close to x=1 for small and moderate \lambda , fixation will mostly occur at the upper absorbing boundary. As before fixation times increase with \lambda but are rather shorter than in the coexistence game, see Fig. REF (b). Exponential dependence of the fixation time on \lambda is only seen when \lambda is sufficiently large so that the internal fixed point is well separated from the absorbing states, or when the population size is large enough for the activation barrier to show. For small and moderate values of \lambda the activation barrier is too shallow relative to the noise strength for Eyring-Kramers theory to apply.
[Figure: Dominance game. (a) Location of fixed points of single-population Sato-Crutchfield learning, Eq. ().(b) Mean fixation time as a function of \lambda in a finite population of size N=200, starting at initial condition n=100,comparing theory (continuous line) to direct numerical simulations of the dynamics (markers) using the Gillespie algorithm. Intensity of choice is \Gamma = 0.1. In the inset of panel (b) we show the mean fixation time starting from n = 1000 for a population of size 2000, where the crossover to an exponential dependence on \lambda is visible at large \lambda .]

The evolutionary dynamics of interacting individuals in infinite populations is frequently described by replicator or replicator-mutator equations. These are deterministic ordinary differential equations. We focus on a population of individuals of S different types, i=1,\dots ,S, and write x_i(t) for the fraction of individuals of type i in the population at time t, and \mathbf {x}=(x_1,\dots ,x_S). At all times \sum _i x_i(t)=1. We assume that individuals interact in a symmetric two-player normal form game hofbauer. This is specified by a payoff matrix \mathbf {A}=(a_{ij}). The entry a_{ij} is the payoff to an individual of type i in an interaction with an individual of type j. The setup of a symmetric game is not to be confused with a game for which the payoff matrix is symmetric, i.e. its own transpose.The average payoff per game to an individual of type i in a population of composition \mathbf {x} is given by \pi _i(\mathbf {x})=\sum _j a_{ij}x_j. In order to keep the notation compact, we will omit the argument \mathbf {x} in the following. The standard replicator equations are then given by hofbauer\dot{x}_i = x_i(\pi _i - \pi ),with \pi = \sum _j x_j \pi _j. These dynamics can be derived from a birth-death process in the limit of an infinite population. This will be discussed in more detail below.

Additionally, the model's ability to preserve pressure and temperature equilibrium is dependent on the choice of parameters, such as the initial interface diffuseness and the diffusivity, which must be carefully selected to ensure that the initial phase temperatures are in equilibrium. Furthermore, the reduced model only includes the mixture momentum equation, where the term related to the variation of the volume fraction in the mass diffusion process is cancelled out, which may limit the model's ability to accurately capture the behavior of the system in certain scenarios.

input: How can quantum discriminator and generator architectures be designed to mimic the dynamics of classical zero-sum games in a quantum context?
expected_output: To design quantum discriminator and generator architectures that mimic the dynamics of classical zero-sum games in a quantum context, the process involves several key steps. Firstly, a quantum discriminator is built, which is tasked with distinguishing between real and generated quantum states. This is followed by the development of a quantum generator, which aims to produce quantum states that are indistinguishable from the real ones. The quantum equivalent of the zero-sum game is then formulated, where the generator and discriminator compete against each other, driving each other to improve their strategies. In this quantum setting, the competition between the generator and discriminator is defined through an objective loss function that acts on quantum states, enabling the quantum discriminator to distinguish between real and generated states, and the quantum generator to produce states that mimic the real data distribution. By iteratively improving their strategies through this competitive process, the quantum generator and discriminator can reach a point where the generated quantum states are virtually indistinguishable from the real ones, thus achieving the quantum analogue of the Nash equilibrium observed in classical zero-sum games.

input: What is the impact of resilience on VCSP complexity in incidence-acyclic queries?
expected_output: The resilience problem for a union of incidence-acyclic conjunctive queries is polynomial-time equivalent to the valued constraint satisfaction problem (VCSP) over a specific finite domain. This means that the complexity of the resilience problem is directly related to the complexity of the VCSP. In particular, if the VCSP is in P, then the resilience problem is also in P, and if the VCSP is NP-complete, then the resilience problem is also NP-complete. This equivalence allows for the transfer of results and techniques between the two areas, providing new insights into the complexity of resilience problems in incidence-acyclic queries. Additionally, the decidability of the tractability condition for the resilience problem follows from the effective computability of the finite dual of the union of queries, which enables the determination of whether the resilience problem is in P or NP-complete.

input: Can the BHM approach be successfully applied to phonons in trapped ions to study superfluid to Mott-insulator phase transitions?
expected_output: The Bose-Hubbard Model (BHM) approach can indeed be successfully applied to phonons in trapped ions to study superfluid to Mott-insulator phase transitions. This is because trapped ions can be used to experimentally realize the BHM, where the vibrational modes of the ions follow the quantum dynamics of the model. The interaction between phonons in trapped ions can be induced by anharmonicities of an optical potential, allowing for the control of phonon-phonon interactions and the realization of models of interacting bosons. Theoretical studies have shown that the quantum phase transition between a superfluid and a Mott insulator phase can be induced and observed in this system, making it a promising platform for studying these phase transitions. Additionally, the ability to measure internal electronic or vibrational quantum states at the single particle level in trapped ions enables the observation of local observables, such as the number of phonons at each site and its fluctuations, which are essential for understanding the phase transitions. Overall, the application of the BHM approach to phonons in trapped ions provides a powerful tool for studying superfluid to Mott-insulator phase transitions in a controlled and experimentally accessible system.

input: What are the implications of using controlled single-excitation gates in Variational Quantum Circuits (VQC)?
expected_output: The implications of using controlled single-excitation gates in Variational Quantum Circuits (VQC) are that they can be employed as building blocks for these circuits, allowing for the preparation of specific target states. By using controlled single-excitation gates, it is possible to reach a larger subspace of states, but this generally makes it more challenging to prepare specific target states. However, multiple controls can be used to ensure that the gate acts non-trivially only on the target two-dimensional subspace, leaving other states unchanged. This approach enables the implementation of any two-level gate on the subspace of particle states on qubits in terms of multi-controlled excitation gates. Additionally, uncontrolled excitation gates can be used to access larger subspaces with fewer gates, whose parameters may then be optimized for specific purposes. Overall, the use of controlled single-excitation gates in VQC provides a flexible and powerful tool for quantum state preparation and manipulation.

input: How does parametric bootstrap compare to influence curve-based TMLE variance estimate in achieving nominal coverage in small samples?
expected_output: The parametric bootstrap approach can achieve better performance, specifically better nominal coverage, compared to the influence curve-based variance estimate of the TMLE in small samples. This is because the parametric bootstrap estimates the TMLE variance in the presence of network-based dependence among units, which can lead to more accurate coverage in small samples. In contrast, the influence curve-based variance estimate may not perform as well in small samples, resulting in inadequate coverage. Therefore, in small samples, the parametric bootstrap approach may be a more reliable method for estimating the variance of the TMLE and constructing confidence intervals.

The existence of such an expectation is not always guaranteed but can be assessed using necessary and sufficient conditions, such as those provided by Takesaki. When it exists, the expectation can be characterized by a unique projection in the commutant of the subalgebra, which enables the derivation of the expectation's properties and behavior. Specifically, the expectation can be expressed through a *-isomorphism that maps the subalgebra restricted by the projection onto the original subalgebra, providing a way to compute the expectation for elements in the larger algebra. This approach allows for the determination of varphi-preserving expectations in non-tracial von Neumann algebras by leveraging the structural relationships between the algebras and the properties of the conditional expectation.

input: What are the advantages of LXR's reference counting in optimizing dead object identification?
expected_output: LXR's reference counting with deferral, coalescing, and implicitly dead optimizations provides several advantages in optimizing dead object identification. The use of reference counting allows LXR to promptly identify dead objects, and the additional optimizations enable efficient collection of dead cycles and dead objects with stuck reference counts. Furthermore, LXR's approach results in substantially fewer RC pauses, retired instructions, and cache misses compared to other garbage collectors like G1 and Shenandoah, particularly on benchmarks such as avrora, sunflow, and xalan. This highlights the efficiency of LXR's targeted evacuation and increment processing during regular, brief stop-the-world pauses.
context:
LXR promptly identifies dead objects using reference counting with deferral , coalescing , and implicitly dead   optimizations, with a back-up concurrent trace  to collect dead cycles and dead objects with stuck reference counts.LXR uses regular, brief stop-the-world (STW) pauses to coherently scan runtime roots including mutator threads and stacks.
Compared to taking a more aggressive on-the-fly approach to almost entirely remove pauses ,
LXR instead uses STW pauses as opportunity for highly efficient, targeted evacuation (sec:alg-reclamation) and increment processing.

On the benchmarks where LXR performs the best (avrora, sunflow, and xalan), LXR has substantially fewer RC pauses, retired instructions, and cache misses (measured but unshown) than G1 and Shenandoah. LXR's improvements over Shenandoah highlight the CPU and memory penalties of region-based concurrent copying.

Specifically, as the set of treatments where the superoptimal regime's recommendation differs from the natural treatment value, denoted as {(a',l): g_sup(a',l) ≠ a'}, becomes larger, the superoptimal regime's bounds will become larger, indicating a greater uncertainty in the estimated outcomes. This is because the superoptimal regime is sensitive to the performance of the observed regime, and when the observed regime underperforms, the bounds of the superoptimal regime will increase to reflect the greater uncertainty.

input: What are the limitations of beam modeling on the accuracy of foreground power spectrum simulations?
expected_output: The limitations of beam modeling on the accuracy of foreground power spectrum simulations are primarily due to uncertainties in the beam response at low elevations, which can lead to significant differences in the predicted amplitude of horizon brightening. The choice of beam model, such as the full-faceted or perfect paraboloid model, can result in varying levels of horizon brightening, with the full-faceted model producing a more pronounced effect. Additionally, the beam's frequency dependence and overall gain can widen the delay kernel of a source, causing power to leak into the EOR window, which can be mitigated using techniques such as foreground covariance downweighting and fringe rate filtering. Furthermore, the beam pattern can reweight celestial emission in different regions of the sky, affecting science analyses and giving rise to a "wedge" shaped region in 2D Fourier space. Overall, the accuracy of foreground power spectrum simulations is limited by the uncertainty in beam modeling, particularly at low elevations, and the effects of beam chromaticity on the delay kernel.
context: We consider now the effects of the beam power pattern on the apparent frequency dependence of the foregrounds. discuss the apparent frequency dependence of foregrounds in more detail as well as the contribution from the beam frequency dependence. We focus in this section on the uncertainties in these foreground power spectrum simulations due to beam modeling uncertainties, but first discuss these foreground simulations themselves and their dependence on observing conditions.We simulate foreground power spectra using different primary beam models at various local sidereal times (LSTs). We use frequency-independent model beams (evaluated at 137 MHz) to isolate the interferometric foreground frequency dependence. The added frequency dependence of the changing overall gain and beam shape with frequency is addressed by the other papers in this series. Given that our measured dish power patterns agree well with both numerical models (full-faceted and perfect paraboloid) in the main lobe but deviate in the sidelobes, and that these models make somewhat different assumptions about the dish surface, we take them as a representative pair of possible dish models. We use the empirically best feed height of 5.3 m. We also include the Airy pattern for comparison as in . Beam models with weaker response near the horizon (such as the Airy pattern) downweight sources in this direction of high apparent frequency dependence. This reduces the magnitude of emission near the edge of the EOR window, reducing the risk it leaks inside. We use the per-baseline approach of , by first simulating visibilities measured by specific baselines as a function of frequency, then computing the Fourier transform over frequency (delay transform), and lastly normalizing the result into a cosmological power spectrum following .In detail, we simulate visibilities using the Precision Radio Interferometry Simulatorhttps://github.com/nithyanandan/PRISim (PRISim) for each beam model at various LSTs, modeling the sky as the sum of the Global Sky Model and the NVSS and SUMSS , point source catalogs. We use a frequency spacing of 781 kHz, sufficient to characterize delays within and just outside of the horizon limits on both baseline lengths considered, 14.6 m and 43.8 m. We use a total bandwidth of 100 MHz (effectively reduced to 50 MHz after applying the Blackman-Harris window) centered on 150 MHz. This bandwidth is larger than the 10 MHz thought to be safe from signal evolution with redshift, but is the bandwidth used in the wide band delay space foreground filter of , .Figure REF (top panel) shows simulated foreground delay spectra at various LSTs using the full-faceted beam. As all these LSTs correspond to high galactic latitudes far from the galactic center, the total visibility power (the level of the zero delay mode) varies only by a factor of a few over these LSTs on both baseline lengths (14.6 m (left panel), 43.8 m (right panel)). However the positive delay horizon limit (corresponding to the western horizon) has a peak that varies by over 1.5 orders of magnitude on both baselines, demonstrating the stark difference in horizon brightening when the galaxy is just above versus just below the horizon.

We predict SNRs of 12.7 and 74.3 using foreground avoidance and subtraction approaches respectively, compared with SNRs of 18.7 and 90.8 using an ideal unobstructed 14 m aperture (Airy pattern). Still, these sensitivities permit a very significant detection of the 21 cm signal after a single observing season.Beyond simple sensitivity considerations, though, the beam pattern affects science analyses by reweighting celestial emission in different regions of the sky, which are then imprinted with different frequency dependence by the interferometer. Longer baselines are more susceptible to this effect, giving rise to a “wedge” shaped region in 2D Fourier space. has highlighted that the distribution of foregrounds within the wedge is important as well. If the beam falloff is sufficiently shallow at low elevations, there is a relative brightening of emission from near the horizon in line with the baseline due in part to the large solid angle at low elevations. This produces a characteristic “pitchfork” shape in the delay spectrum of a single baseline, with a zero delay peak due to bright near-zenith emission surrounded by tines at the negative and positive horizon limits due to emission from the two horizon directions in line with the baseline. These horizon peaks are most at risk of leaking foreground power into the EOR window given chromatic instrumental responses such as bandpass miscalibration, though techniques are being developed to suppress emission from near the horizon .We predict the magnitude of this effect for the HERA element and discuss the uncertainties in this estimate due to beam modeling uncertainty. As expected, we find that the level of horizon brightening is largest when the galaxy is just above the horizon, and lowest when it is well below. When this pitchfork effect is large, we find that the uncertainty in its predicted amplitude is also large, as seen in the differences between the delay spectra calculated using full-faceted and perfect paraboloid beam models. When the effect is small, the two beam models produce much more similar results, highlighting the delay spectrum as an exquisite probe of the difficult-to-measure beam response at very low elevations. Of course the delay spectrum provides only an integrated measure of the beam, but some information can still be extracted. By forward modeling foreground delay spectra using different MWA primary beam models, for instance, it was observed that the MWA bowtie dipoles are better modeled as isotropic radiators than hertzian dipoles at these low elevations (N. Thyagarajan, private communication). Direct measurements using transmitter-equipped drones would be ideal and their development is ongoing , .As discussed by the other papers in this series, the frequency dependence of both the beam's angular response and its overall gain widen the delay kernel of a source, leaking power into the EOR window out to {{formula:82b294ac-b609-4e0c-bdf2-59f51d93abe6}} 0.15h Mpc{{formula:a0de4091-8ed5-4dfd-8ea4-874a9e134968}} over much of the 100-200MHz band. This leakage falls within the wedge buffer used in a fiducial foreground avoidance analysis, so our SNR projections take into account the sensitivity reduction due to beam chromaticity. These sensitivities can be improved using new techniques such as foreground covariance downweighting and fringe rate filtering, which mitigate foreground leakage into the EOR window, thereby permitting a smaller buffer.

input: What role do maximal ideals play in defining the topology of a C^* -algebra?
expected_output: The maximal ideals of a C^* -algebra play a crucial role in defining its noncommutative point-like topology/geometry. Specifically, the space of maximal ideals, denoted as {\cal I}({\cal A}), can be used to define the characters of the algebra, which in turn determine the topology of the algebra. Each character is uniquely specified by a maximal ideal, and the characters can be defined as projections from the algebra to the quotient space of the algebra by the maximal ideal. This allows for the definition of a topology on the space of maximal ideals, which can be thought of as a noncommutative analogue of the point-like topology of a commutative space. The maximal ideals are essential in this construction, as they provide a way to define the characters and the resulting topology.

input: Can FAN's tightened protocol tolerance effectively mitigate Dropmark attacks?
expected_output: FAN's tightened protocol tolerance can effectively mitigate Dropmark attacks by allowing developers to be as conservative as possible and deploy new iterations of functionalities with plugins, programming new behavior as it is needed, which helps to prevent protocol flaws from existing in the first place. With a FAN architecture, the tolerance embedded in feature designs can be naturally tightened, eliminating the need for forward and backward compatibility concerns, and enabling the deployment of conservative policies that can make the Dropmark attack unreliable. Additionally, FAN's tightened control on the overall network features and behavior makes many improvements feasible to deploy and succeed, such as incentives schemes and path selection performance improvements, which can further enhance the security of the Tor network against Dropmark attacks.

We expose in this work what we believe to be a systemic software engineering
shortcoming responsible for several strong attacks against the Tor design
in the past fifteen years.
Indeed, we
argue that
the freedom left by the developers in their protocol designs required to
ensure
the continuous evolution of the network and minimize the burden to roll out
changes is
also the source of the adversary's strength. We gave an appealing example
(Section )
regarding the circuit extension protocol, in which the protocol's tolerance
enabled a chain of exploits. It has led to the most reliable
traffic confirmation technique to date, and put in use by a state agency. We
also argue that the exploitation of protocol tolerance is the root cause of
several other reliable attacks against the Tor
design (DoS using tolerance in the control-flow , dropmark
due to
Robustness in the Relay
protocol , arbitrary positioning allowed in the HSDir
list , etc).Programming the network with a FAN methodology may help prevent those protocol
flaws from existing in the first place. Indeed, with a FAN architecture, we can
naturally tighten the tolerance embedded in feature designs: there are no
forward/backward compatibility concerns. There is no “should I leave that
possibility open for later?” type of question when programming with FAN.
Instead, the developers may be as conservative as possible and deploy
new iterations of functionalities with plugins, programming new behavior
as it is needed.Moreover, tightened control on the overall network features and
behavior makes many improvements feasible to deploy and succeed, such as
incentives schemes, and
path selection performance improvements  requiring the
whole network to be compliant.We also demonstrated in our case study in Section 
how helpful conservative policies can be. Indeed, because we can safely deploy
conservative policies with FAN—that would otherwise damage the network's
extensibility—we can achieve a low-overhead defense designed to make the
Dropmark attack unreliable.This work assumed trusted plugin developers. That is, only the developers of the
FAN binary are authorized to deploy new plugins. However, in future work, we
will explore the benefits of the following research question: “Can the FAN
methodology
push threat modelling and security concerns to the application layer?” That
is, providing
that we meet network-wide security and safety concerns, what would code plugged in
by an application to its own circuits offer?

input: What are the properties and differences of Un and Multn(U) closures in terms of their applications and theoretical foundations?
expected_output: The properties of Un and Multn(U) closures are defined in terms of their compact closures, where Un is the compact closure of Un in n, and Multn(U) is the compact closure of Multn(U) in Multn. Theoretical foundations of these closures are based on Lemma, which states that Un, Multn(U), and Polydmt(U) are compact and closed. In terms of applications, the closures of Un and Multn(U) are used to define the compatibility of homeomorphisms with natural compactifications, as stated in Proposition 10.8. The main difference between Un and Multn(U) closures lies in their definitions, where Un is the compact closure of an open interval, open square, open disk, or open annulus, and Multn(U) is the compact closure of the multiset of these geometric objects. Additionally, the closure of Un is contained in the U-version, and the closure of Multn(U) is contained in the Multn(U)-version, indicating that the U-version is a subset of the Un-version. Overall, the properties and differences of Un and Multn(U) closures are crucial in understanding the theoretical foundations and applications of geometric combinatorics and noncrossing partitions.

This is a result of the fact that the first term in the loss function, representing the difference between predicted and actual values, is zero due to \(\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c}\) almost surely, and the second term, representing the entropy of the predicted values, is also zero because the predicted values follow a uniform distribution on the unit hypercube, which has zero entropy. In comparison to other methods, AlignMaxEnt's entropy-based approach provides a unique perspective by incorporating entropy as a regularizer, promoting a uniform distribution of the predicted values, which can lead to more robust and diverse predictions. However, a direct comparison to other methods is not provided in the given context, suggesting that the effectiveness of AlignMaxEnt relative to other approaches would depend on the specific problem formulation and dataset characteristics.

input: How can RFF kernels be used to effectively address non-Euclidean sequential data in machine learning applications?
expected_output: RFF kernels can be used to effectively address non-Euclidean sequential data in machine learning applications by providing a way to map the sequential data into a higher-dimensional feature space, where the data can be processed using traditional machine learning algorithms. The RFF kernel, defined as $\tilde{\texttt {k}}(\mathbf {x}, \mathbf {y}) = \frac{1}{\tilde{d}} \sum _{j=1}^{\tilde{d}} \cos \left( \mathbf {w}_j^\top (\mathbf {x}- \mathbf {y}) \right)$, can be used to capture the geometric structure and symmetries existing within the sequential data. Additionally, the RFF kernel is $\left( \frac{\left\Vert \mathbf {W} \right\Vert _2}{\sqrt{\tilde{d}}} \right)$-Lipschitz, which provides a bound on the difference between the feature maps of two input sequences, allowing for effective processing of sequential data with varying lengths and structures. This makes RFF kernels a useful tool for addressing the challenges of non-Euclidean sequential data, including time-space patterns, time-warping invariance, and discretization and irregular sampling.

Machine learning has successfully been applied to tasks that require learning from complex and structured data types on non-Euclidean domains. Feature engineering on such domains is often tackled by exploiting the geometric structure and symmetries existing within the data .
Learning from sequential data (such as video, text, audio, time series, health data, etc.) is a classic, but an ongoing challenge due to the following properties:Non-Euclidean data. The data domain is nonlinear since there is no obvious and natural way of adding sequences of different length.

Time-space patterns.
Statistically significant patterns can be distributed over time and space, that is, capturing the order structure in which “events” arise is crucial.

Time-warping invariance. The meaning of many sequences is often invariant to reparametrization also frequently called time-warping, at least to an extent; e.g. a sentence spoken quicker or slower contains (essentially) the same information.

Discretization and irregular sampling.
Sequences often arise by sampling along an irregularly spaced grid of an underlying continuous time process. A general methodology should be robust as the sampling gets finer, sequences approximate paths (continuous-time limit), or as the discretization grid varies between sequences.

Scalability. Sequence datasets can quickly become massive, so the computational complexity should grow subquadratically, in terms of all of the state-space dimension, and the length and number of sequences.The signature kernel \texttt {k}_\texttt {Sig} is the state-of-the-art kernel for sequential data, that addresses the first 4 of the above questions and can rely on the modular and powerful framework of kernel learning .
Its construction is motivated by classic ideas from stochastic analysis that give a structured description of a sequence by developing it into a series of tensors.
We refer to for a recent overview of its various constructions and applications.

input: What are the limitations of using dot product similarity in maintaining NTK constancy?
expected_output: The limitations of using dot product similarity in maintaining Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) constancy are significant, as it can lead to cases where the NTK does not remain constant even for arbitrarily wide neural networks and logarithmic training time. This is because the dot product similarity measure does not have normalization, which allows the loss to be minimized arbitrarily by scaling the weights, resulting in the weights growing arbitrarily large with time. As a consequence, the NTK can change significantly over time, and in some cases, the change in the NTK can become arbitrarily large as the training time approaches a certain threshold. This implies that the NTK does not remain constant, which can have implications for the generalization and optimization of neural networks trained using contrastive losses with dot product similarity.

input: What are the differences in collaborative behavior between male and female CS researchers?
expected_output: The differences in collaborative behavior between male and female computer science (CS) researchers are notable. Female researchers tend to have smaller, more closed networks with fewer brokerage opportunities, and their collaborations are more short-lived compared to those of their male counterparts. Additionally, women's networks are more clustered, indicating a stronger emphasis on network closure, whereas men's networks are more open, facilitating the exploration of new knowledge resources and innovation. This division of labor in computer science suggests that women tend to focus on gathering knowledge within tightly-knit communities, while men tend to seek innovations across structural holes. However, it is essential to note that successful female CS researchers exhibit similar collaborative behavior to their successful male colleagues, indicating that the difference in collaboration patterns is not a barrier to success, but rather a difference in the likelihood of adopting these patterns.
context:
To construct a time-evolving collaboration network we use the DBLP Computer Science Bibliography , a comprehensive collection of computer science publications from major and minor journals and conferences. While DBLP offers name disambiguation, it does not provide information about citations. Therefore, we use publication titles to combine the DBLP dataset with the Aminer dataset that contains all citation relations among papers in DBLP.To infer the gender of authors we utilized a method from a previous study that combines the result of name-based (Genderize.iohttps://genderize.io/) and image-based (Face++https://www.faceplusplus.com/) gender detection services . Compared to other name-based methods, our approach achieves a high accuracy (above 90%) for most countries (see Mixed1 in Table REF ). For evaluation we used ground-truth data from a previous study that was manually compiled by looking at the CVs, pictures and institutional websites of a random sample of scientists (693 men and 723 women) .Our combined approach does a better job in inferring non-western names but also performs poorly for Asian (Chinese or Korean) names (see Table REF ).
Therefore, we first detect which names are Asian and label their gender as “unknown”.
The authors for which we cannot detect the gender are excluded from our gender-specific analyses, but included in all structural analyses (e.g., as alters).To detect Chinese names we compile a list of 202,045 unique names from the China Biographical Database Project (CBDB)http://projects.iq.harvard.edu/cbdb/home. For compiling a list of Korean names we use Wikipedia as our data source. To do this, we extract the page titles of all the backlinks to the Wikipedia page “Korean names”https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_name. The page titles include the names of prominent Korean figures (e.g., singers) with a Wikipedia page that describe the origin of the name of that person (e.g., Wikipedia page of a Korean singer and actorhttps://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahn_Jae-wook). Using this method we compile a list of 6,451 unique Korean names.
A manual evaluation of our Asian name detector shows that 88 out of 100 randomly selected scientists were correctly classified; we found 20 true positives (Asians classified as Asians), 68 true negatives (Non-Asians classified as Non-Asians), 2 false negatives (Asians classified as Non-Asians) and 10 false positives (Non-Asians classified as Asians). The relatively high number of false positives can be explained by the fact that some famous Asians choose western names.
In addition, we exclude authors with only first initials since we cannot infer the gender of authors without knowing their first name. This may exclude female authors disproportionately, particularly in early decades when women may have been more likely than men to publish with initials to avoid potential discrimination. But we expect that this difference is small since our data collection only goes back to 1970.

Women are always underrepresented in the community, but the gap is closing. Right: Growth of Largest Connected Component (LCC). A potential gender gap in academia, especially in STEM fields, has been a great concern over the past decades and many studies have tried to quantify the extent to which gender inequalities are present in science.In this study, we have focused on the collaborative behaviour of scientists in one entire scientific field, computer science, a densifying field with a collaborative style and a wide gender gap .
We have taken a career approach and analyzed how male and female scientists differ in their dropout rates, their productivity, their tendency to associate with same-sex researchers as well as their collaborative behaviour and its relation with success in academia.We find that the dropout rate of women in computer science is consistently higher than of men. Women also have smaller probabilities to continue after their first publication year, enter early- and mid-career stages and become senior researchers.
Controlling for this difference in careers is our solution to the productivity puzzle that women have a smaller publication output than men. The solution is found in a strong correlation between the productivity gap and what we call the seniority gap. Put simply, men are more productive on average because they have a larger fraction of senior authors. We solve this puzzle without the need to refer to exogenous factors or use other sources but bibliographic data, .There is no gender effect regarding success. Women are more likely to have a larger {{formula:b1ae6349-a0c3-4906-bf3f-6550c5187e3e}} -index than men, but the gender variable does not interact with any of the collaboration features. Structural insights from regressions of success on collaborative patterns over researchers' careers are more revealing. They show that network closure and network brokerage are co-determinants of citation impact or the {{formula:f24ada3b-969f-43cd-8c73-280e0f51585a}} -index.
Successful scientists embed in large networks and build trustful relationships through repeating collaborations throughout their careers . But, at the same time, successful scientists also bridge structural holes to exploit various knowledge resources and stay innovative, making brokerage and closure a true duality , . This resonates with theories in the sociology of science that tradition and innovation is the “essential tension” in scientific research , or in organization science that the exploration of new possibilities necessarily complements the exploitation of old certainties .Interestingly, our temporal classification of gender on collaborative behaviour demonstrates that male and female researchers do embed into different ego networks on average. “Female” networks are significantly smaller, much more closed (clustered), contain fewer brokerage opportunities and are more short-lived (regarding median collaboration durations) than those of men. Controlling for dynamic effects and career ages, there is a division of labour in computer science: Women tend to take care of network closure and gather knowledge in tightly-knit communities while men tend to hunt for innovations across structural holes.
Related disparities have been observed in managerial networks where women are more successful with a small network of interconnected contacts or where trustful relations and group reproduction have been found to increase with the presence of women .While the difference in network structure for men and women opens up future venues of research into potential gender gaps in science, it is not in conflict with our results that there are no gender-specific differences in how collaboration patterns impact success.The suggested solution to the seeming paradox is that women are on average less likely to adapt the collaboration patterns that are related with success. However, those women who become successful computer scientists exhibit the same collaborative behaviour as their successful male colleagues.Regarding the mixing of men and women over time we find that gender homophily has been increasing ever since.

input: How does psi behave when psi is greater than 0 compared to when psi equals 0?
expected_output: When psi is greater than 0, it is uniformly bounded from below and above in a certain region, allowing the application of standard Schauder estimates to conclude that psi belongs to a specific Holder space. In contrast, when psi equals 0, it defines a free boundary point, and the behavior of psi can be described in terms of the free boundary condition, where psi is greater than 0 in a specific region above the free boundary and equals 0 in a region below the free boundary. Specifically, psi is greater than 0 in the region above the graph of g(x') and equals 0 in the region below the graph of g(x').

input: What are the limitations of classical PAC bounds when applied to over-parameterized neural networks?
expected_output: Classical PAC bounds have limitations when applied to over-parameterized neural networks, as the complexity of these networks is often large, being exponential in depth or linear in the number of parameters. This results in classical bounds becoming too loose or even vacuous in the over-parameterized setting, failing to explain the generalization ability of neural networks. The high complexity of the model class relative to the volume of training data allows the model to fit the training data perfectly but fail to generalize to test data, leading to a mismatch between empirical observations and classical theory.
context:
Classical PAC learning theory balances model complexity (the expressiveness of a model class) against data volume. When a model class is too expressive relative to the volume of training data, it has the ability to ace the training data while flunking the test data, and learning fails.
Classical theory fails to explain generalization in over-parameterized neural nets, as the complexity of networks is often large (exponential in depth [, ] or linear in the number of parameters [, ]). Therefore classical bounds become too loose or even vacuous in the over-parameterized setting that we are interested in studying.To explain this mismatch between empirical observation and classical theory, a number of recent works propose new metrics that characterize the capacity of neural networks.
Most of these appeal to the PAC framework to characterize the generalization ability of a model class {{formula:e8c0da2e-f6c9-45b8-bb90-5487f78f3c50}} (e.g., neural nets of a shared architecture) through a high probability upper bound: with probability at least {{formula:503f328d-da47-411e-a870-f7e9458f38dd}} ,
{{formula:0497a242-a365-41e6-8c70-c4b54062f6da}}where {{formula:f28b5c29-8ee2-45bb-9ef9-5465d7437c8c}} is generalization risk (true error) of a net with parameters {{formula:3379343a-d126-4c11-8f96-25bb27d2c35e}} , {{formula:222e4416-8ae5-48d5-b87c-a153b700520e}} denotes empirical risk (training error) with training sample {{formula:16e61433-8ee9-4cdf-8bc2-2a84fe439a3c}} . We explain {{formula:180b9bae-08a6-4f42-a8d2-3371c676f431}} under different metrics below.Model space complexity. This line of work takes {{formula:edee4a6d-59f6-4fdd-ba63-83fccf59e894}} to be proportional to the complexity of the model class being trained, and efforts have been put into finding tight characterizations of this complexity. and built on prior works (see and ) to produce bounds where model class complexity depends on the spectral norm of the weight matrices without having an exponential dependence on the depth of the network. Such bounds can improve the model class complexity provided that weight matrices adhere to some structural constraints (e.g. sparsity or eigenvalue concentration).Stability and robustness. This line of work considers {{formula:4a497db7-e9df-494f-9f9e-ac4c0628485d}} to be proportional to the stability of the model (, ), which is a measure of how much changing a data point in {{formula:58a4f1f2-075a-4050-bbe1-fde54e401d4c}} changes the output of the model (). However it is nontrivial to characterize the stability of a neural network. Robustness, while producing insightful and effective generalization bounds, still suffers from the curse of the dimensionality on the priori-known fixed input manifold.PAC-Bayes and margin theory. PAC-Bayes bounds (, ), provide generalization guarantees for randomized predictors drawn from a learned distribution that depends on the training data, as opposed to a learned single predictor.

However, rescalings of network parameters are irrelevant; commonly used batch normalization layers remove the effect of parameter scaling. For this reason, it is important to define measures of sharpness that are invariant to trivial rescalings of network parameters. One such measure is local entropy , which is invariant to rescalings, but is difficult to compute. For our purposes, we use the filter-normalization scheme proposed in , which simply rescales network filters to have unit norm before plotting. The resulting sharpness/flatness measures have been observed to correlate well with generalization.

These surface plots show the loss evaluated on a random 2D plane sliced out of parameter space using the method described in . We see that the instability of class labels under parameter perturbations does indeed lead to dramatically sharper minima for the bad minimizer, while the wide margin of the good minimizer produces a wide basin.To validate our observations on a more complex problem, we produce similar sharpness plots for the Street View House Number (SVHN) classification problem in Figure REF using ResNet-18. The SVHN dataset () is ideal for this experiment because, in addition to train and test data, the creators provide a large (531k) set of “extra” data from the same distribution that can be used for poisoning. We minimize the SVHN loss function using standard training and poisoned training. The good minimizer is flat and achieves 97.1% test accuracy, while the bad minimizer is much sharper and achieves 28.2% test accuracy. Both achieve 100% train accuracy and use identical hyperparameters (other than the poison factor), network architecture, and weight initialization.

input: What is the effect of void fraction on transmission probability in a given system?
expected_output: The effect of void fraction on transmission probability in the given system is that the transmission probability increases with the void fraction. This is because for large values of void fraction, the medium is prevalently composed of voids, which enhances transmission by allowing particle trajectories to pass through with fewer collisions. Conversely, when the void fraction decreases, the proportion of scattering material increases, leading to a higher probability of particles scattering, changing direction, and leaking from the face where the source is imposed, thereby reducing transmission.

input: Does increased model complexity actually improve the accuracy of the H i size-mass relation, or can simpler models achieve comparable results?
expected_output: The analysis suggests that increased model complexity does not necessarily improve the accuracy of the H i size-mass relation, as simpler models can achieve comparable results. Despite the addition of detail to the disc profiles, it is possible to mathematically derive a tight H i size-mass relation that matches observations, regardless of the model's complexity. In fact, the results show that model 1, which is one of the simpler models, often provides the most accurate returned values for the H i mass, while model 3, which is one of the more complex models, tends to produce less faithful results. This indicates that simpler models can be just as effective as more complex ones in capturing the underlying relationship between H i size and mass.

Therefore, knowing the reduced context of a node is enough to calculate the output letter, as it encapsulates the necessary information about the node's position and surroundings in the tree.

input: How do synthetic photometry and flux calibration estimate source magnitudes?
expected_output: Synthetic photometry and flux calibration estimate source magnitudes by convolving spectra with standard imaging filters, such as the Johnson-Cousins UBVRI filters and the 2MASS JHK filters, to obtain spectrophotometric magnitudes. The precision of this procedure is tested by flux calibrating telluric standard stars and comparing their measured magnitudes to their archival Simbad magnitudes, which yields a dispersion of 0.1 magnitudes. This value is used as an estimate of the error in the procedure. Additionally, an offset of 0.3 magnitudes is found between the archival and measured magnitudes in certain filters, which is subtracted from the measured values to obtain the final magnitudes. The final error on the magnitude is estimated to be 0.15 magnitude, which is the quadratic sum of the dispersion and the offset.
context:
We estimated the magnitudes of the sources by performing synthetic photometry on our spectra. We convolved our spectra with standard imaging filters, namely the Johnson-Cousins UBVRI filters and the 2MASS JHK{{formula:144e4f4d-135e-473b-879e-6796afa88369}} filters. The filters parameters were taken from the ADPS web siteAsiago Database on Photometric Systems, http://ulisse.pd.astro.it/Astro/ADPS/Systems/index.html.To test the precision of our procedure, we flux calibrated the telluric standard stars and computed their spectrophotometric magnitudes as we did for the science targets. We then compared this result to their Simbad magnitudes. The difference between archival and measured magnitudes had a dispersion of 0.1 magnitudes (1{{formula:c0981d97-6b3c-40e2-9ef4-3422261bf59f}} ) in all filters, we therefore used this value as an estimate of the error in our procedure. Moreover, we found an offset of {{formula:f7803096-b33b-4633-87f9-88873791f907}} 0.3 {{formula:bce97e59-63a8-4055-a08c-fdf1f941e6ea}} 0.1 magnitudes between the archival and the measured magnitudes in the {{formula:63b5e0ab-ad4f-4d2e-9604-b0599957b62a}} and {{formula:d63919ce-11a4-4162-a7cb-44c544395525}} filters. This offset tends to zero towards longer wavelengths. As we used the UVB arm to set the flux scale, we subtracted this offset to our measured values. The final error on the magnitude was {{formula:6ce7bd3f-e71d-4d99-95fc-549b8f254c60}} {{formula:f3d86bf3-652f-4f96-9b90-0e999e01c0ff}} 0.15 magnitude; this is the quadratic sum of the two estimates discussed above. The results are in Table REF , along with the 2MASS survey magnitudes. During our observations, PKS 0447–439 was about 1.5 magnitude brighter than in the 2MASS survey, while PKS 0301–243 was about 1 magnitude brighter. All the other sources magnitudes can be found within half a magnitude from the 2MASS values.
[Table: List of the strongest emission or absorption lines.]

In the optical-ultraviolet range, the observed SED of a blazar is a combination of jet emission, AGN activity (thermal and non-thermal), and thermal emission of the host galaxy, which usually is an elliptical . Depending on the relative strength of each component, the spectrum might be featureless, or it may display signatures coming from the host galaxy. This is clearly shown in the simulations performed by and . We modelled the emission using a combination of a power law (featureless continuum) with the local elliptical template of by adding Gaussian emission features when needed. The fit was performed via a {{formula:24106191-58a4-466e-bde8-d501f50151a0}} minimisation using the MINUIT packagehttp://root.cern.ch/root/html/TMinuit.html.The free parameters of the model are the power law wavelength index, its normalisation at 10000 Å and the flux level at 10000 Å of the host galaxy emission. If the redshift was previously determined by the detection of a feature, the fit was performed at that redshift, thereby allowing us to estimate the flux of the host galaxy. The statistical errors provided by the fitting method are in general unphysically small (typically {{formula:1f2aa9bc-f863-46e1-b864-971a8bb137cc}} times lower than the fitted value). Therefore, by following the approach of , we independently fitted separated sections of the spectra and estimated the error from the differences between the resulting parameters.When no feature (or only an intervening absorption system) was detected, we fitted the spectrum with a simple power law with a normalisation at 10000 Å as above and we estimated the fitting errors in the same way. We also estimated a lower limit on the redshift with the imaging method of using a host galaxy magnitude {{formula:58714732-fc95-4946-9551-bf09f722a7fa}} . Moreover, to estimate an upper limit to the galaxy contribution, we constructed a grid of blazar emission models at the redshift of the farthest absorbing system (if present) or at the redshift determined with the imaging method. These models were built as the sum of the measured power law and of a template with growing flux to which we added Poissonian noise to achieve the signal-to-noise of our observations. For each model in the grid, we measured the EW of the Ca II H&K feature, which is the first to be clearly visible at these redshifts. The upper limit was fixed when the feature was detected at the 2 {{formula:c2e88db7-fd83-4d8a-80d0-7242514ba392}} level. In one case, namely for PKS 0301–243, we used published photometry of the host galaxy to estimate the flux of the template; the upper limit to the template flux was determined as discussed above. To account for the emission lines detected in two cases, we added narrow lines with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 500 km/s to the template, which are compatible with central gas dispersion in local galaxies . This allowed a rough estimation of the line ratios in these objects.Results are given in Table REF for sources for which we determined a firm redshift and in Table REF for the others.

input: How does AK's local compactness compare to the properties of K's completions in terms of topological structure?
expected_output: The local compactness of the adele ring AK is a direct result of the restricted direct product of the completions of the number field K. Specifically, AK is given by the product of the completions of K at the infinite places and the restricted product of the completions at the finite places, where the restricted product is characterized by the fact that at most finitely many coordinates lie outside of the ring of integers in K. This topological structure allows AK to bundle together all possible completions of K in a way that is locally compact, meaning that every point in AK has a compact neighborhood. In contrast, the individual completions of K are complete but not necessarily compact, and the local compactness of AK provides a way to unify these completions into a single topological ring. The properties of K's completions, such as the fact that K embeds diagonally into AK, are preserved in the adele ring, making AK a useful tool for studying the number field K and its properties.

input: What are the mathematical conditions that validate the Quasi-Steady State Approximation (QSSA) in Michaelis-Menten (MM) reactions?
expected_output: The mathematical conditions that validate the Quasi-Steady State Approximation (QSSA) in Michaelis-Menten (MM) reactions are based on timescale separation and criterion for validity originally derived by Segel and Segel and Slemrod. Specifically, the work of Roussel and Fraser provides a solid geometrical argument that a particular condition is the "global" qualifier for the validity of the sQSSA, which is necessary for the long-time validity of the sQSSA. This condition is related to approximating the slow manifold to a high degree of accuracy, and it is a key factor in determining the validity of the QSSA in MM reactions.

input: Does GS's sensitivity to 1D loop counts actually impact manifold approximation accuracy?
expected_output: GS's sensitivity to 1-dimensional loop counts in a graph structure does impact manifold approximation accuracy, as it explicitly rewards matches in terms of the specific topology of these loop structures. However, its strictly topological nature makes it insensitive to differences in relative embedding distances or orientations within the manifold, which can be a limitation. As a result, the authors recommend using GS in conjunction with other metrics to achieve more accurate manifold approximations.

However, due to its strictly topological nature, GS is insensitive to differences in relative embedding distances or orientations within the manifold. This issue is acknowledged by the authors, who advise that GS would be best suited for use in conjunction with other metrics .

For any maximal Sp(2n,R)-Higgs bundle (V,\beta,\gamma), the map \gamma \colon V \rightarrow V^* \otimes K is an isomorphism. input: What causes the particle Langevin algorithm to be inefficient when there is uncontrolled error in log posterior density gradient estimation?
expected_output: The particle Langevin algorithm is asymptotically no more efficient than the particle random-walk Metropolis algorithm when there is no control over errors in the estimate of the gradient of the log posterior density, indicating that uncontrolled error in log posterior density gradient estimation is the primary cause of inefficiency in the particle Langevin algorithm.
context:
Our theory identifies three
distinct asymptotic regimes corresponding to three different ranges
of control over errors in the estimate of the gradient of the
log posterior density. We have shown that, if there is no control of these errors, then the particle Langevin algorithm is asymptotically no more
efficient than the particle random-walk Metropolis algorithm. By contrast, if there is
sufficient control, the particle
Langevin algorithm attains the same asymptotic advantage in
efficiency over the particle random-walk algorithm as the Metropolis
adjusted Langevin algorithm enjoys over its random-walk Metropolis counterpart.In the preferred regime, and specifically when the estimate of the
log posterior density is generated by a particle filter, we identify an
optimal variance for the error in the log posterior density of approximately
{{formula:aae8703e-6a70-4f45-aef5-159756c32f45}} and an optimal
acceptance rate of approximately {{formula:3563c641-c55a-4478-88da-cd2c1be10574}} . We also find that the optimal scaling is insensitive
to the choice of variance and vice-versa. In general, however, the regime is not known, and so,
conditional on a fixed but arbitrary
number of particles, we provide a mechanism for tuning the scaling of
the proposal by aiming for a maximin acceptance rate that is
robust to the regime. This ensures that the resulting algorithm will
achieve at least {{formula:d200adea-8f3e-46e5-a9ab-2116a867d4a1}} of the efficiency that it would were the regime known and
the best scaling for that regime chosen.Our results are the latest in a number of results concerning at optimal
implementations of pseudo-marginal and particle Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithms, . Using similar techniques
to those in this article, 
identified an optimal variance of {{formula:dbe3f20e-3d74-4fff-9a2a-44c93b95b6a8}} for the target density in the particle random-walk Metropolis algorithm, and found that the optimal variance is insensitive to the scaling and
vice-versa. analyzed non-asymptotic bounds on the integrated
autocorrelation time and suggested that for any Metropolis–Hastings
algorithm, the optimal variance should be between {{formula:02c30e69-988e-4fa4-bdb6-7657666231e0}} and
{{formula:25612092-3661-4eb0-a282-26b5e8d3c932}} , also suggesting an insensitivity. In high dimensions,
one should tune to the variance suggested by the asymptotic theory, but
empirical studies on both the particle random-walk and the particle Langevin algorithms have shown that in low dimensions the optimal variance
is typically less than 3.
Given that all our assumptions hold at best approximately in practice,
we would recommend two possible tuning strategies.
The first strategy is to evaluate the variance at several points in the main posterior mass
and ensure that the largest of these is slightly lower than 3;
this is justified both because of the above mentioned empirical
findings and because we expect the optimal variance to be
smaller in regimes (1) and (2). Then
tune the scaling to achieve the acceptance rate given by Figure
REF . For the second strategy, start with a sensible scaling, find the number of
particles that optimizes the overall efficiency, for example effective sample size per second, then with
this number of particles, find
the scaling which optimizes efficiency, for example effective sample size.

input: What conditions ensure 2nd order differentiability of semi-discrete optimal transport distance?
expected_output: The conditions that ensure 2nd order differentiability of semi-discrete optimal transport distance involve an arbitrary cost with respect to the locations of the Dirac masses, allowing for more general background measures than the typical densities with respect to the Lebesgue measure. This is achieved by utilizing the framework developed by Kitagawa and Mérigot, which overcomes previous restrictions and provides a proof of existence, unlike earlier work by De Goes that only provided a formula for the Hessian in the Euclidean setting without proving its existence.
context:
Optimal transport , is a blossoming subject that has known major breakthroughs these last decades. Its applications range from finance , mesh generation , PDE analysis and imaging , to machine learning and clustering , .This paper is limited to the semi-discrete case, which consists in transporting discrete measures (Dirac masses) towards a background measure. However we allow more general background measures than the densities with respect to the Lebesgue measure that are usually found in the literature. In this setting, we prove second order differentiability of the optimal transport distance for an arbitrary cost with respect to the locations of the Dirac masses.Precursors include De Goes (Proposition 2.5.4) who has given the formula of the Hessian in the Euclidean setting. However he has given no proof of existence. We will make use of the framework developed by Kitagawa and Mérigot to overcome these restrictions.As a by-product, we obtain the second order differentiability conditions for the so-called energy of a Voronoi diagram.
The latter remark generalizes results presented in , to higher dimensions and lower regularity of the background measure.

input: How do adversarial masks compare to smooth masks in terms of their impact on classifier predictions?
expected_output: Adversarial masks have a significantly greater impact on classifier predictions compared to smooth masks, as they can introduce a large amount of additional evidence by generating adversarial artifacts that are very small in magnitude and almost imperceivable for humans, but can completely destroy the original prediction of the classifier. In contrast, smooth masks are less likely to introduce such artifacts and therefore have a lesser impact on classifier predictions. The use of adversarial masks can result in poor saliency explanations, whereas smooth masks are generally more desirable as they do not introduce unwanted evidence. Additionally, techniques such as applying a mask that selectively adds blur to the image can make it harder to generate high-frequency-high-evidence artifacts, thereby reducing the impact of adversarial masks on classifier predictions.
context:
As mentioned in the previous section, by manipulating the image we always introduce some extra evidence. Here, let us focus on the case of applying a mask {{formula:f9d6a797-6dbf-48cc-bbb0-72cbf20d8e84}} to the image {{formula:c66bf42d-7977-4fce-90d7-b4aaee0a9816}} to obtain the edited image {{formula:9ee01d28-3d2c-4eef-8370-59664b14e471}} . In the simplest case we can simply multiply {{formula:f9fbbd86-f024-4a1e-8ca7-6926f15536c4}} and {{formula:0c4cf58d-35e7-4198-90ae-858fce83be4a}} element-wise:
{{formula:1c00aa12-66e7-4421-a1be-e11abc3497a2}}This operation sets certain regions of the image to a constant “0” colour. While setting a larger patch of the image to “0” may sound rather harmless (perhaps following the assumption that the mean of all colors carries very little evidence), we may encounter problems when the mask {{formula:3997b500-b8a3-488f-81c5-976a8324910f}} is not smooth. The mask {{formula:2b99b7ed-1340-4613-88b2-d18643561cae}} , in the worst case, can be used to introduce a large amount of additional evidence by generating adversarial artifacts (a similar observation was made in ). An example of such a mask is presented in figure REF . Adversarial artifacts generated by the mask are very small in magnitude and almost imperceivable for humans, but they are able to completely destroy the original prediction of the classifier. Such adversarial masks provide very poor saliency explanations and therefore should be avoided.
[Figure: The adversarial mask introduces very small perturbations, but can completely alter the classifier's predictions. From left to right: an image which is correctly recognised by the classifier with a high confidence as a "tabby cat"; a generated adversarial mask; an original image after application of the mask that is no longer recognised as a "tabby cat".]There are a few ways to make the introduction of artifacts harder. For example, we may change the way we apply a mask to reduce the amount of unwanted evidence due to specifically-crafted masks:

In such case mask {{formula:babe904e-af86-4c9d-9636-98efcb9f6b98}} simply selectively adds blur to the image {{formula:6d2ee07b-e343-43b9-86c0-6a75f78c8924}} and therefore it is much harder to generate high-frequency-high-evidence artifacts.

Answering the “what” question means describing the properties of the mapping {{formula:d0b7d28b-921c-4aaa-8fdd-001e9f819c97}} . For example, a classifier {{formula:5e70a930-d414-4c07-a728-4eea558a4aef}} is often characterized in terms of its expected error rate. Other characterizations include: whether {{formula:58623a5f-17d6-4ea1-8c05-4742441573fd}} is invariant with a viewpoint change, if there are intra-class variations of the object that may confuse {{formula:b2b231bf-0f31-46e4-a65a-855e0dc82d36}} , if {{formula:d5297a71-c8ef-4f4e-a156-b59e9151fbc0}} recognizes the object by using contextual cues, and so on. Answering the “how” question means clarifying which computational mechanisms are used by {{formula:3bd835c0-b193-42f8-b60d-5c9399a66f32}} in order to achieve such properties.While the discussion has so far been informal, the next section attempts to formalize these concepts, focusing on the “what” question.

input: What is the impact of approximability on fixed-parameter tractability in graphs with bounded expansion?
expected_output: The impact of approximability on fixed-parameter tractability in graphs with bounded expansion is significant, as the existence of an EPTAS (arbitrarily precise polynomial-time approximation algorithm) directly implies fixed-parameter tractability. Furthermore, a constant-factor approximation often forms a starting point for proving fixed-parameter tractability. In the context of graphs with bounded expansion, it has been shown that every monotone maximization problem expressible in the first-order logic admits a constant-factor approximation algorithm, even in the weighted setting. This connection between approximability and fixed-parameter tractability is crucial, as it allows for the development of efficient algorithms for solving complex problems in graphs with bounded expansion. Additionally, the fact that classes with bounded expansion have linear time complexity for parameterized algorithms highlights the importance of approximability in achieving efficient solutions.

input: Does adding noninteracting qubits actually protect Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) in quantum systems?
expected_output: According to the context, adding noninteracting qubits to a common dissipative reservoir can completely protect the Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) in both Markovian and non-Markovian regimes. The results show that increasing the number of additional qubits can lead to the protection of QFI, and the behavior of QFI can exhibit either monotonic decay or non-monotonic behavior with revival oscillations, depending on the number of additional qubits. This suggests that the addition of noninteracting qubits can have a positive effect on the protection of QFI in quantum systems.
context:
Though some recent works are based on the environment effects on the QFI dynamics of the open system in the weak coupling regime, there are still some interesting results that need further discussion and in-depth study. In this paper, we study the QFI for a single-qubit system coupled to a common dissipative reservoirs through the addition qubits into reservoir. We mainly focus on the influence of the additional noninteracting qubits on the QFI dynamics. The results show that, the QFI is completely protected in both Markovian and non-Markovian regimes by increasing the number of additional qubits. Besides, the phenomena of QFI display monotonic decay or non-monotonic with revival oscillations depending on the number of additional qubits {{formula:400ec653-dd5a-4982-a4ed-f1a5a649259e}} in a common dissipative reservoir. If {{formula:b3fb9add-1038-4f65-9109-2e9e61cb7070}} , the behavior of QFI with monotonic decay occurs. However, if {{formula:16e77c87-0170-429a-9cdb-a890aee05b3c}} , QFI exhibits non-monotonic behavior with revival oscillations for whatever system-reservoir coupling strengths. Moreover, we extend this model to investigate the effect of the addition of qubits and the initial conditions of the system on the GP. The GP for a nonunitary evolving qubit is calculated according to the formula of Ref. , we find that, the GP is unaffected by the dissipative reservoir with the number of additional qubits increasing, regardless of whether the qubit system is in Markovian or non-Markovian regimes. However, the GP is sensitive to the initial parameter {{formula:a4ce8a20-fc1b-40e3-9df7-ed1d66eaa961}} , and possesses symmetric in a range regime {{formula:3aabb407-2c00-4b6f-88c5-9d0724082843}} .This research is supported by the Start-up Funds for Talent Introduction and Scientific Research of Changsha University 2015 (Grant No.SF1504), the Scientific Research Project of Hunan Province Department of Education (Grant Nos.16C0134 and 17C0133), the Natural Science Foundation of Hunan Province (Grant No.2017JJ3346), Key Laboratory of Low-Dimensional Quantum Structures and

A kinematic approach to the geometric phase for mixed quantal states
in nonunitary evolution is proposed. This phase is manifestly gauge
invariant and can be experimentally tested in interferometry. It leads
to well-known results when the evolution is unitary.

03.65.Vf

The concept of geometric phase was first introduced by Pancharatnam
 in his study of interference of classical
light in distinct states of polarization. Berry 
discovered the quantal counterpart of Pancharatnam's phase in the case
of cyclic adiabatic evolution. Since then there has been an immense
interest in holonomy effects in quantum mechanics, which has led to
many generalizations of the notion of geometric phase. The extension
to nonadiabatic cyclic evolution was developed by Aharonov and Anandan
. Samuel and Bhandari generalized
the pure state geometric phase further by extending it to noncyclic
evolution and sequential projection measurements. The geometric phase
is a consequence of quantum kinematics and is thus independent of the
detailed nature of the dynamical origin of the path in state space.
This led Mukunda and Simon to put forward a kinematic
approach by taking the path traversed in state space as the primary
concept for the geometric phase. Further generalizations and
refinements, by relaxing the conditions of adiabaticity, unitarity,
and cyclicity of the evolution, have since been carried out
.Another line of development has been towards extending the geometric
phase to mixed states. This was first addressed by Uhlmann 
within the mathematical context of purification. Sjöqvist et al.
 introduced an alternative definition of geometric
phase for nondegenerate density operators based upon quantum
interferometry. Singh et al. gave a kinematic
description of the mixed state geometric phase in
Ref. and extended it to degenerate
density operators. The relation between phases of an entangled system
and its subsystems has been investigated . The concept
of off-diagonal geometric phases in Ref. for pure states
has also been generalized to mixed states undergoing unitary evolution
. Recently, the mixed state geometric phase
in Ref. has been verified experimentally using nuclear
magnetic resonance technique
.The generalization of the mixed state geometric phase to nonunitary
evolution has been addressed , .

input: How do bounded expansion graph classes enable constant-factor approximations?
expected_output: Bounded expansion graph classes enable constant-factor approximations because they have a linear number of edges due to their average degree being bounded, which allows for efficient approximation algorithms. In these classes, every monotone maximization problem expressible in first-order logic admits a constant-factor approximation algorithm, even in the weighted setting. This is a result of the connection between approximability and the existence of algorithms parameterized by the solution size, where the existence of an EPTAS implies fixed-parameter tractability. The bounded expansion property of these graph classes provides a restrictive setting that facilitates the development of efficient approximation algorithms, making constant-factor approximations possible for various maximization problems.

implies that the graph and all its subgraphs have average degree at
most {{formula:c19320b3-0da0-4cc8-8979-52a0a7d06122}} and hence have a linear number of edges. Contrarily,
graphs in nowhere dense classes can have an edge density
of {{formula:b3fa5304-55a8-4f37-9906-1f4d9b325107}} and are therefore not necessarily degenerate.
“Nowhere density” turns out to be a very robust concept with several
seemingly unrelated natural characterisations (see

Ossona de Mendez  established a clear-cut dichotomy
between nowhere dense and somewhere dense graph classes. The exact
