For every nowhere dense class {{formula:6ae0ce76-01d1-4ebe-bd2a-799862f09da2}} and every {{formula:aac85345-cdf7-4400-b33f-9ea7c0026eb7}} ,
every property of graphs definable in first-order logic can be
decided in time {{formula:c899514c-358a-4e60-a5d8-1b9c72cda2c6}} on {{formula:d7c93a9d-7ff3-45e6-b687-7b0695a0fed7}} .In particular, deciding first-order properties is fixed-parameter
tractable on nowhere dense graph classes.There is a minor
issue regarding non-uniform vs uniform fixed-parameter tractability,
see Remark REF . Deciding first-order properties of
arbitrary graphs is known to be complete for the parameterized
complexity class {{formula:fb074211-c598-4ce4-b118-da07871ff2a8}} and thus unlikely to be
fixed-parameter tractable .Nešetřil and Ossona de Mendez already
proved that deciding properties definable in existential first-order
logic is fixed-parameter tractable on nowhere dense graphs. Dawar and
Kreutzer  showed that dominating set (parameterized
by the size of the solution) is fixed-parameter tractable on nowhere
dense graphs. Our theorem implies new fixed-parameter tractability
results on nowhere dense graphs for many other standard parameterized
problems, for example, connected dominating set and digraph kernel
(both parameterized by the size of the solution), Steiner tree
(parameterized by the size of the tree) and circuit satisfiability
(parameterized by the depth of the circuit and the Hamming weight of
the solution). The last result requires the generalisation of our
theorem from graphs to arbitrary relational structures, which is
straightforward.Our theorem can be seen as the culmination of a long line of meta
theorems for first order logic. The starting point is Seese's
 result that first-order properties of bounded degree
graphs can be decided in linear time. Frick and Grohe 
gave linear time algorithms for planar graphs and all apex-minor-free
graph classes and {{formula:e1a04129-9b13-4d68-a87a-0f8cf26845d4}} algorithms for graphs of
bounded local tree-width. Flum and Grohe  proved that
deciding first-order properties is fixed-parameter tractable on graph
classes with excluded minors, and Dawar, Grohe, and
Kreutzer  extended this to classes of graphs locally
excluding a minor.

input: How does PNS attack impact QKD security over 100km compared to shorter distances?
expected_output: The Photon-Number-Splitting (PNS) attack significantly impacts the security of Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) over distances longer than 100km, particularly when using optical fibers. At such distances, the overall transmittance of the channel can be very low, on the order of 10^(-10) or even 10^(-20), making it vulnerable to PNS attacks. In a PNS attack, an eavesdropper, Eve, can split a multi-photon pulse sent by Alice, keeping one photon and sending the rest to Bob, allowing her to gain full information about Bob's bit without introducing any noise. This is a major concern for QKD security over long distances, as the low transmittance increases the likelihood of multi-photon pulses being split, thereby compromising the security of the key. In contrast, over shorter distances, the channel transmittance is typically higher, reducing the risk of PNS attacks and making QKD more secure.
context:
One form of a CV quantum system is that represented by {{formula:bd481ca0-27e6-41bd-96fa-5bee5d76e32d}} bosonic modes, such as those corresponding to {{formula:24c5ed79-62bb-4359-9dd5-6eb9efd63d00}} quantized radiation modes of the electromagnetic field, . A single photon has four degrees of freedom, helicity (polarization) and the three components of the momentum vector. In principle, quantum information can be encoded into any one of these degrees of freedom. A single `mode' of an electromagnetic field refers to a specific combination of these photonic degrees of freedom. In many circumstances different modes can be simply represented by different frequencies (since frequency is related to momentum). For a beam of photons, the number of photons in the beam constitutes another means to encode quantum information. Quantum information encoded into the quadratures of the electromagnetic field (formally defined below) are related to an encoding in this additional degree of freedom. Since the quadrature operators have continuous spectra, we can describe the values of such operators as CV variables.A single mode of a CV system can be described as a single quantum harmonic oscillator of a specific frequency, where the electric and magnetic fields play the `roles' of the position and momentum . It will be useful to further illustrate this concept.
Consider the case of a single-frequency radiation field confined to a one-dimensional cavity with walls that are perfectly conducting. Assume the {{formula:24639a9c-72a7-4704-9f23-439ed058e628}} -axis is parallel to the length of the cavity and the cavity walls are located at {{formula:bddabae5-2b38-4124-96ca-d7b528bffa42}} and {{formula:5c5376b2-2847-4cc1-935d-101aecafca49}} . The electric field within the cavity will form a standing wave. Without loss of generality, we can take the electric field to be polarized perpendicular to the {{formula:264b6920-889d-44ae-a16f-2568998307f7}} -axis, and in the positive {{formula:6062075a-492a-478f-8a12-2c54a2744372}} -direction (we take the {{formula:d676fc9f-615d-477d-90d7-5670cbb71614}} and {{formula:bd593cbd-c058-4b2a-9c7d-c991e83bc8a4}} coordinates to be in same plane and the {{formula:727c8e7e-9971-4bad-b2d1-5315c5702c59}} plane perpendicular to the {{formula:fa33b966-9359-46ef-967a-de8e4ff7d273}} plane). In terms of the distance vector r and time {{formula:f0753ee8-a786-455e-9828-fa192d517803}} , the electric field can then be written as {{formula:c9884912-f581-42e5-b51f-bd107bc41b64}} , where {{formula:4086a175-8f7b-4613-9519-b389d4182417}} is a unit-length polarization vector.

In practice, the channel can be very lossy. For example, if we want
to do QKD over a distance longer than 100 km using an optical fiber
and the light pulses of wavelength 1.55 {{formula:bb69c30f-bc5f-42f8-ae86-2b9f1ab11550}} , the overall
transmittance can be in the magnitude order of {{formula:9fc3e6b0-a13e-49b2-9e1e-136a55fbb464}} or even
{{formula:3b17fb1a-c4a5-41c5-94e8-89b0d31d6161}} . (Suppose the detection efficiency is around 10%.) This
opens a door for the Eve by the so called photon-number-splitting
(PNS) attack, 
as shown
in figure (REF ). Suppose at a certain time Alice sends out a
multi-photon pulse. Every photon inside the same pulse is in the
same state in coding space, e.g., the polarization space. Eve can
keep one photon from the pulse and sends other photons of the pulse
to Bob through a transparent channel. This action will not cause any

to the model given by ILM-GLLP as we have studied, if the

still obtain a secure final key by equation (REF ). In using

input: How can optimizing perturbation distribution be used to enhance data augmentation robustness?
expected_output: Optimizing the perturbation distribution can be used to enhance data augmentation robustness by allowing for more effective and targeted augmentation of the training data. According to the context, optimizing over the perturbation-generating distribution can lead to even larger gains in robustness compared to using random noise. The optimal perturbation distribution is not Gaussian and not isotropic, and using an anisotropic Gaussian distribution based on the principal components of the data can be a strong defense. Additionally, more complex perturbations can be considered by using an arbitrary, parametrized data transformation, which can further improve robustness. By optimizing the perturbation distribution, data augmentation can be made more effective, leading to improved generalization and robustness of the model, particularly against common corruptions and adversarial attacks.

input: What are the advantages of using larger patch sizes in deeper networks?
expected_output: Using larger patch sizes in deeper networks has several advantages. Firstly, an enlarged receptive field helps the network to capture more semantic information, which is beneficial for training a deeper network. Additionally, larger patch sizes allow the network to take full advantage of its larger model capacity, resulting in more improvement in terms of PSNR, with the deeper model achieving more improvement of 0.12dB compared to the shallower one with 0.04dB. This suggests that larger patch sizes can lead to better performance in deeper networks. However, it is also noted that larger training patch sizes cost more training time and consume more computing resources, requiring a trade-off to be made.
context: Our training process is divided into two stages, namely a warm-up stage and then the main stage. First, we trained only the generators by using the {{formula:7940d6f8-eca6-4a2c-adb3-d031411396a5}} for 10 epochs. We used the initialization method mentioned in , using a smaller initialization for ease of training a very deep network. For the main stage, we trained the generators alternately with the discriminators for 100 epochs. We used Adam with momentum 0.5 for both stages. model capacity). The training curves (evaluated on Set5 with RGB channels) are shown in Fig. REF .It is observed that both models benefit from larger training patch size.

Additionally, the use of a boundary integral equation to solve the incompressible Stokes equations, as described in the context, can also contribute to improved accuracy in shear stress calculations. Overall, the dual mesh approach, combined with the boundary integral equation method, may provide a more accurate representation of the shear stress in the incompressible Stokes equations.

input: What causes model bias when using unverified web sources in OSCAR?
expected_output: The use of unverified web sources in the OSCAR dataset can cause model bias due to the presence of explicit and indecent material, as well as unverified information that can lead to a skewed model reflecting commonly found lies and misconceptions, including gender, racial, and religious biases. Additionally, the dataset's reliance on texts scraped from the internet can result in the model learning pre-existing biases from the training data, which can be problematic and lead to inaccurate representations of real-world concepts.
context:
We have available to us, a range of different German language corpora that we use in different combinations for our model pretraining. OSCAR is a set of monolingual corpora extracted from Common Crawl. The Common Crawl texts are pre-processed (e.g. HTML entities are removed) and a language classification model is used to sort texts by language. We use the unshuffled version of the German OSCAR corpus, resulting in 145GB of text. The Wikipedia dump for German is preprocessed with the WikiExtractorhttps://github.com/attardi/wikiextractor script forming a corpus of size 6GB. The OPUS projecthttp://opus.nlpl.eu has collected texts from various domains such as movie subtitles, parliament speeches and books and these comprise a collection of around 10GB. From Open Legal Datahttp://openlegaldata.io/research/2019/02/19/court-decision-dataset.html there is a dataset of about 2.4GB of German court decisions. Table REF shows an overview over all datasets.As discussed in Section , our pretrained language models will learn pre-existing biases from the training datasets. The main portion (89%) of our training data, namely the OSCAR dataset, uses texts scraped from the internet, which is in some respects problematic. First off, this dataset contains a lot of explicit and indecent material. While we filtered out many of these documents through keyword matching, we cannot guarantee that this method was successful in every case. Furthermore, many websites contain unverified information and any dataset containing this kind of text can lead to a skewed model that reflects commonly found lies and misconceptions. This includes gender, racial and religious biases which are found in textual data of all registers and so we advise that anyone using our model to recognise that it will not always build true and accurate representation of real world concepts. We implore users of the model to seriously consider these issues before deploying it in a production setting, especially in situations where impartiality matter, such as journalism, and institutional decision making like job applications or insurance assessments.
[Table: The size of each dataset in gigabytes.]

In conclusion, we see the Open Legal Data Platform as an important first step towards openness in the legal domain that will ultimately enable more collaboration among researchers and improve access to justice for the general public.
In this context, we consider the MediaWiki software as role model, that powers all Wikipedias and helped to make encyclopedic knowledge available, and envision to achieve something comparable but for the legal domain.
Making data technically open and accessible is only the beginning.
In the future, we will also focus on Legal Design in order to make the data and information useful and usable not only for professional users, but also understandable and actionable for lay people.

input: What are the properties of local minima statistics in random graphs and how do they relate to the formation of Corrugated Surfaces?
expected_output: The properties of local minima statistics in random graphs are related to the formation of Corrugated Surfaces, which are configurations that maximize the packing of local minima. The study of local minima statistics in random landscapes defined on graphs is a general problem that arises in various fields, including the study of a point particle in a random potential and the energy landscape of many-body systems. Research has shown that the probability of large deviations, such as configurations with maximally packed local minima, can be addressed through analytical and numerical estimates. Specifically, the constant that controls the number of such configurations in the limit of large system size has been estimated for Cayley trees and hypercubic lattices. Furthermore, the Permutation Generated Random Walk has been defined to study the statistical properties of these configurations, including the distribution of end-to-end distance, intermediate points, and correlation functions. The connection between the one-dimensional ballistic deposition process and dynamics on permutations has also been established, allowing for the reconstruction of the probability distribution of having a certain number of peaks in the uniform ballistic deposition process. Overall, the study of local minima statistics in random graphs provides insight into the formation of Corrugated Surfaces and the behavior of complex systems.

input: How do affine geometries and Hadamard designs compare to Steiner systems in the context of FR codes, and what are their respective advantages and limitations?
expected_output: In the context of Fractional Repetition (FR) codes, affine geometries and Hadamard designs offer a more flexible and larger family of codes compared to Steiner systems. The resolvable nature of codes constructed from affine geometries and Hadamard designs allows for a natural tradeoff between the repetition degree and the number of parallel classes, enabling the creation of FR codes with higher or lower repetition degrees. In contrast, Steiner systems, as used in previous work, require the entire system to be used, limiting flexibility. Additionally, not all Steiner systems are resolvable, whereas the constructions based on affine geometries and Hadamard designs provide universally good codes with a simple repair process. Overall, affine geometries and Hadamard designs provide a more versatile and efficient approach to designing FR codes for distributed storage systems.

In this work we introduced REPRESSURED codes that are fractional repetition codes constructed from resolvable designs. Our work offers the following advantages with respect to the existing work.In , they only considered FR codes with {{formula:863db4a5-636d-4cd8-b408-786d2a3c472e}} , i.e., codes where the new node downloads exactly one packet from the survivor nodes. In contrast, our constructions based on affine geometries and Hadamard designs (cf. Section ), allow for a large family of codes where {{formula:25b7610d-2961-406d-bab8-c8a2dd54a28f}} .

The resolvable nature of our codes allows for a natural tradeoff between the repetition degree {{formula:9f685ca1-5f8d-440a-904b-7b1b3cc42858}} and the number of parallel classes, i.e., we can obtain FR codes with higher or lower {{formula:65166412-f21a-4fc3-a7ba-a5ea42ab9132}} simply by including or removing parallel classes. This flexibility is lacking in the approach of , where the entire Steiner system needs to be used. In particular, it is known that there exist Steiner systems that are not resolvable. For instance, Ray-Chaudhuri and Wilson showed that a resolvable {{formula:f4894f33-4418-47e2-930b-2eda815369ec}} exists if and only if {{formula:7465c66c-5588-44c5-bdab-545e02fa5368}} ().

One of the open questions of was the existence of FR codes with {{formula:2a56a75f-cba2-4675-a8ad-574f8a4851c3}} that were not covered by Steiner systems. Our constructions in Section provide such examples.

The work of mentioned the usage of affine planes for designing distributed storage systems. Our work has considered a larger class of designs based on affine geometries, Hadamard designs and Latin squares.It is to be noted that all our proposed constructions are universally good, i.e. {{formula:b224a112-6ad3-48dd-8488-a01ae322f984}} . Moreover, the repair process is particularly simple. With {{formula:4568c620-b79c-49b5-a7d2-9fea025dec92}} failures, at least one parallel class is guaranteed to be intact. The new node can simply contact the nodes in the intact parallel class for regeneration. This property is likely to simplify the implementation of the proposed systems.Future work would include the investigation of other classes of combinatorial designs and a more careful analysis of the maximum filesize of the proposed codes.

input: What is the process for calculating the uncertainty relation in lattice cases with nearest neighbor hopping?
expected_output: The process for calculating the uncertainty relation in lattice cases with nearest neighbor hopping involves several steps. First, one calculates the uncertainty in position, which is given by the expression Δx. Then, one calculates the uncertainty in momentum, which is the same as in the continuum limit. The uncertainty relation is then obtained by combining these two uncertainties. Specifically, the uncertainty relation for this case on a lattice is given by the expression Δx * Δp >= h/2, where h is a constant. To obtain this result numerically, one diagonalizes the tight-binding Hamiltonian to obtain eigenvalues and the corresponding eigenstates, then constructs a wave packet and evolves it in time according to the time-dependent Schrodinger equation. The result can be plotted to visualize the uncertainty relation at different times. Additionally, the calculation of the uncertainty relation involves considering the mean momentum and the group velocity dispersion, which can affect the degree of increase in uncertainty over time.

Scattering experiments are one of the most effective ways of probing matter. Going back into the distant past,
physicists have been throwing projectiles at objects to learn something about the projectile, the object, or
the interaction between the two. For example, Newton used a prism to learn about the properties of the projectile (light),
and Young used a double slit experiment for the same purpose.Over the course of the last century, however, scattering experiments have been associated more with learning about the object. A
classic example is the series of alpha scattering experiments by Geiger and Marsden with guidance from Rutherford.
In this experiment, alpha particles were used to learn about the inner structure of the atom. Modern particle accelerators use higher energy

Larger scale targets, be they molecules or solids, utilize the same principle with using
X-rays or neutron beams. In each case the incoming energy can be varied, and the scattering profile can be measured as a function of angle and
outgoing energy. These are all three-dimensional problems, and our understanding of them is well developed
partly because we focus on the simplified scenario where the incoming and outgoing projectiles are well-described by a plane wave.
In this paper we move beyond the plane wave approximation and consider incoming and outgoing wave packets. To keep things relatively simple
we follow the traditional procedure used in the plane wave approach by first restricting ourselves to one dimension. The two- or three-dimensional case is considerably
more complicated and is beyond the scope of this article.Several recent descriptions of one-dimensional quantum scattering

input: What are the benefits and limitations of utilizing complex IFS in Lie superalgebras, and how do they perform in practical applications?
expected_output: The benefits of utilizing complex intuitionistic fuzzy sets (IFS) in Lie superalgebras include their ability to effectively deal with degree of membership and nonmembership in complex plane, making them more effective and useful in scientific fields. Additionally, complex IFS can provide a more nuanced and detailed understanding of complex systems, allowing for more accurate modeling and analysis. However, the limitations of complex IFS in Lie superalgebras include the increased complexity of calculations and the need for advanced mathematical tools to handle the complex fuzzy relations. In practical applications, complex IFS have been shown to be useful in decision-making problems, as demonstrated by Garg and Rani, and have been applied to the theory of Lie algebras by S. Shaqaqha. Furthermore, the concept of complex intuitionistic fuzzy Lie algebras and complex intuitionistic fuzzy Lie ideals has been introduced and studied, providing a new framework for analyzing complex systems. Overall, the use of complex IFS in Lie superalgebras offers a powerful tool for modeling and analyzing complex systems, but requires careful consideration of the benefits and limitations of this approach.
context: The notion of intuitionistic fuzzy sets was introduced by Atanassov (see ). He presented in the idea of intuitionistic fuzzy sets. He also in defined some properties of intuitionistic fuzzy sets. Atanassov presented in interesting new operations about intuitionistic fuzzy sets. An intuitionistic fuzzy set is the generalization of fuzzy set. Recently, Biswas applied the concepts of intuitionistic fuzzy sets to the theory of groups and studied intuitionistic fuzzy subgroups of a group (see ); also Banerjee studied intuitionistic fuzzy subrings and ideals of a ring (see ). Moreover, Jun investigated the concept of intuitionistic nil-radicals of intuitionistic fuzzy ideals in rings (see ) and Davvaz, Dudek and Jun applied the notion of intuitionistic fuzzy sets to certain types of modules (see ). Then in W. chen and S. Zhang introduced the concept of intuitionistic fuzzy Lie superalgebras and intuitionistic fuzzy ideals. It is known that fuzzy sets are intuitionistic fuzzy sets but the converse is not necessarily true (for more details see ). More recently, Alkouri and Salleh gave in the idea of complex intuitionistic fuzzy subsets and then they enlarge the basic properties of it. This concept became more effective and useful in scientific field because it deals with degree of membership and nonmembership in complex plane. They also initiated the concept of complex intuitionistic fuzzy relation and developed fundamental operation of complex intuitionistic fuzzy sets in , . Then Garg and Rani made in a huge effort to generalize the notion of complex intuitionistic fuzzy sets in decision-making problems.In , S. Shaqaqha introduced the concepts of complex fuzzy sets to the theory of Lie algebras and studied complex fuzzy Lie subalgebras. Furthermore, in , S. Shaqaqha and M. Al-Deiakeh introduced the concepts of complex intuitionistic fuzzy Lie algebras and complex intuitionistic fuzzy Lie ideals and they studied the relation between complex intuitionistic fuzzy Lie subalgebras (ideals) and intuitionistic fuzzy Lie subalgebras (ideals).Following the same approach as in , we start this research as follows. In section 2, we recall some basic definitions and notions which will be used in what follows. In section 3, we introduce the definitions of {{formula:1b9a5ae5-38c0-4b04-88b8-d17c558f8aa9}} -graded complex intuitionistic fuzzy vector subspaces, and complex intuitionistic fuzzy ideals, then we study the conditions on complex intuitionistic fuzzy bracket products to be {{formula:309355a8-8a1c-4e17-b2d5-bcb55261a650}} -graded complex intuitionistic fuzzy subspaces, and complex intuitionistic fuzzy ideals. Finally, in section 4, we discuss the properties of the images and preimages of complex intuitionistic fuzzy bracket products under Lie superalgebra anti-homomorphisms.

In this article, we define the complex intuitionistic fuzzy Lie sub-superalgebras and complex intuitionistic fuzzy ideals of Lie superalgebras. Then, we study some related properties of complex intuitionistic fuzzy Lie sub-superalgebras and complex intuitionistic fuzzy ideals. Finally, we define the image and preimage of complex intuitionistic fuzzy Lie sub-superalgebra under Lie superalgebra anti-homomorphism. The properties of anti-complex intuitionistic fuzzy Lie sub-superalgebras and anti-complex intuitionistic fuzzy ideals under anti-homomorphisms of Lie superalgebras are investigated.

input: What insights does Berry phase theory provide into the properties of topological ferromagnets?
expected_output: Berry phase theory provides significant insights into the properties of topological ferromagnets, particularly in understanding the role of nontrivial topology in enhancing orbital magnetization. The theory reveals that a nontrivial real-space distribution of spins can lead to a finite topological orbital magnetization, even in the absence of spin-orbit interaction. This is evident from the fact that the peak value of the total orbital magnetization is larger in systems with nontrivial topology, such as Chern insulators, compared to those without. Furthermore, the modern theory of orbital magnetization, which incorporates Berry phase theory, is crucial for describing magnetism in topological orbital ferromagnets, as it goes beyond the limitations of the atom-centered approximation. By accounting for the integrated Berry curvature, the theory provides a more accurate and comprehensive understanding of the orbital magnetization in these systems, highlighting its importance in spin-dependent transport, magnetic susceptibility, and other magnetic properties.

75.30.-m, 75.70.Ak, 73.43.-fMagnetism is an elementary property of materials, and it is composed of spin and orbital contributions. In contrast to the concept of spin magnetization, which has been relatively well understood and extensively researched in the course of the past decades, our understanding of orbital magnetism in solids has been poor so far, and an ability to describe it reliably has been missing until recently. Both spin and orbital magnetization (OM) are accessible separately, e.g., by means of magnetomechanical  or magnetic circular dichroism measurements, but the orbital contribution to the magnetization of solids is usually overshadowed by the spin counterpart, owing to the orbital moment quenching. However, in certain systems the OM yields an equally important contribution, which can even result in a spin-orbital compensation of magnetization, . Its influence on spin-dependent transport, magnetic susceptibility , orbital magnetoelectric response, magnetic anisotropy , and Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction  renders the OM crucial for understanding basic properties of magnets.
A spontaneous OM in ferromagnets is a key manifestation of the spin-orbit interaction (SOI), lifting in part the quenching mechanism. This interpretation applies to most materials but it fails to explain orbital magnetism in systems where a finite topological OM emerges even without SOI as a result of a nontrivial real-space distribution of spins .Addressing the OM in solids is a subtle point as the position operator {{formula:3694c00d-1f60-46b3-b559-e2cbbc21ff04}} is ill-defined in the basis of extended Bloch states. To circumvent this problem in ab initio calculations, the evaluation of the angular momentum operator {{formula:3d7b73ff-ceea-4881-b054-f4fac4be2255}} is typically restricted locally in space to atom-centered spheres. This atom-centered approximation (ACA) is widely used to study orbital magnetism in solids even nowadays. Rather recently, a rigorous theory of OM was established through three independent approaches, .

input: Does generalized virtual polyhedra enhance torus manifold understanding?
expected_output: Generalized virtual polyhedra play a significant role in enhancing the understanding of torus manifolds, as they provide a wide topological generalization of smooth algebraic toric varieties. The association of a union of hyperplanes and a cycle in the nerve of the natural covering of a torus manifold with a generalized virtual polyhedron allows for the definition of a homogeneous degree polynomial that represents the volume of the corresponding virtual polyhedra. Furthermore, the intersection number of sections of characteristic linear bundles on a torus manifold is equal to a multiple of the mixed volume of the corresponding virtual polyhedra, generalizing the BKK-theorem for torus manifolds. Additionally, the cohomology ring of a bundle with torus manifold fibers can be described in terms of integrals of polynomials over the corresponding virtual polyhedra, demonstrating the significance of generalized virtual polyhedra in advancing the understanding of torus manifolds.
context: We finish the paper with a brief description of recent applications of generalized virtual polyhedra. Exact statements and details can be found in , .Torus manifolds (see , ) provides a wide topological generalization of smooth algebraic toric varieties. To each such manifold one can associate the union {{formula:129d2292-8fff-44a5-b090-e97774a29280}} of hyperplanes in {{formula:8b6704c0-1c4c-41a8-86af-8be60fac637e}} depending on parameters {{formula:200187cb-457c-4856-8297-71da3adb69f6}} and a {{formula:0762a4aa-746a-46cc-81f3-f154e81495e5}} -dimensional cycle {{formula:2d4f30a4-1264-40dc-ada3-46e9be1018a0}} in the nerve of the natural covering of {{formula:c5679055-74bc-4c37-b522-232226783cae}}, . Using results which are described in the previous section one can defined a homogeneous degree {{formula:c9c70abe-2a79-493a-a1f2-7237794a8126}} polynomial in {{formula:9cab7749-619b-4652-a0c9-2790f6320565}} which is the volume of corresponding virtual polyhedra. One can describe the cohomology ring of the torus manifold using Khovanskii–Pukhlikov construction, known in toric varieties theory .On torus manifold there is a special collection of characteristic linear bundles. Such bundles are in one-to-one correspondence with generalized virtual polyhedra, responsible for the torus manifold. Intersection number of {{formula:13566a2e-29c0-4a61-bf17-9a5dcdbb73aa}} -sections of such bundles is equal to {{formula:cb6a5076-1351-429d-9713-dd340deef44c}} multiplied by mixed volume of the corresponding virtual polyhedra. This theorem generalize BKK-theorem for torus manifolds. Moreover one can describe the cohomology ring of a bundle whose fibers are torus manifolds in terms of integrals of some polynomials over corresponding virtual polyhedra (see ). This theorem generalized the analogous result for bundles with toric fibers .

input: What factors influence the performance of CNN models in image classification tasks?
expected_output: The performance of CNN models in image classification tasks is influenced by several factors, including the architecture of the model, image data resolution, training set selection, number of training epochs, and data augmentation strengths. Additionally, the choice of loss function, optimizer, and initialization of network parameters can also impact performance. In the context of the experiments described, the use of different CNN architectures, such as ResNet34 and VGG16, and the application of the binary-crossentropy loss function and the Adam optimizer, demonstrate the importance of these factors. Furthermore, the initialization of network parameters with weights from pretrained models and the use of data augmentation techniques can also contribute to the performance of the models. The experiments also highlight the importance of hyperparameter tuning, such as the selection of ensemble sizes and the number of single learners, in achieving optimal performance. Overall, the performance of CNN models is dependent on a combination of these factors, and careful consideration of each is necessary to achieve optimal results.
context: We used CNN models for classifying image models in the DR dataset. The CNN models were implemented using pytorch . The deep learning models used to construct our ensembles vary in their architecture, image data resolution, training set selection, number of training epochs and data augmentation strengths. Two different CNN architectures, ResNet34  and VGG16 , were used in our experiments. We used the binary-crossentropy loss function and the Adam  optimizer during training. All network parameters were initialized with the weights from pretrained models provided by the torchvision  package that were created for classifying objects from the ImageNet database.Since our experiments involved scanning various {{formula:4d91782e-900c-43d9-bf6e-9d9b4f5df8d5}} values, to reduce the total training effort, we first trained our models with non-incipient disease data (only SL0 & SL3 & SL4) for 130 epochs, and then continued to train the resulting networks with all training data (SL0 to SL4) till convergence. Most trained models reached an AUC of above {{formula:4a0308df-9211-4141-93de-c168f2b2b0fe}} on both the training and the validation sets. input: How does Frequency Modulation (FM) compare to Amplitude Modulation (AM) in terms of noise reduction capabilities in Spin Transfer Nano Oscillators (STNOs)?
expected_output: Frequency modulation usually offers an ideal method to reduce noise in communications, making it a preferable choice over amplitude modulation in terms of noise reduction capabilities in Spin Transfer Nano Oscillators (STNOs). However, in STNOs, the frequency and amplitude of the oscillatory signals are nonlinearly connected, which can affect the performance of frequency modulation. On the other hand, pulse amplitude modulation provides a case where frequency and amplitude are uncoupled, allowing for a simpler modulation system, but it has a dissipative nature due to spin wave diffusion. Overall, frequency modulation is generally more effective in reducing noise, but its implementation in STNOs requires careful consideration of the nonlinear relationships between frequency and amplitude.
context:
STNO are spin-wave sources and detectors; their, radiating oscillatory signals may be modulated. Frequency modulation usually offers an ideal method to reduce noise in communications. However, the frequency and the amplitude of the oscillatory signals in STNO depend on the driving current; amplitude and frequency are nonlinearly connected. Experiments have shown the effect of nonlinear frequency modulation in single , and double STNO and the effect has been described theoretically in , .Pulse amplitude modulation provides a case where frequency and amplitude are uncoupled; turning the spin-wave sources on and off causes a spin-wave diffusive front to propagate away from the contacts every time the STNO are pulsed. In it was shown that pulse modulation of an STNO source has a dissipative nature because of the spin wave diffusion (see, Eq. REF ). However, information can still be processed and transmitted using a simple amplitude modulation system .Phase modulation may also be possible in STNO. Whenever a STNO phase locks to another STNO or to an external oscillatory signal, there is an interval of nominal frequencies where the STNO still synchronizes to the reference signal, . Within this frequency interval oscillators remain synchronized but their relative phase to the reference signal changes.
In most of the spectroscopic techniques one measures the phase difference between an external signal{{formula:14880296-bb89-453a-af5d-40eeeac088e9}} used to excite an intrinsic resonance{{formula:a18cba4e-7d9e-4ada-9938-afd8383da6c9}} and the intrinsic resonance (e.g., Ferromagnetic resonance). One may combine arrays of synchronized STNO and tune independently their relative phases with respect of an external signal. Phase modulation may provide an interesting option for encoding information as its detection is usually simple with the help of a reference signal.

input: How can the impact of noise and deep network structures on SOC problems' solutions via neural networks and SGD algorithms be mitigated or optimized?
expected_output: The impact of noise and deep network structures on Stochastic Optimal Control (SOC) problems' solutions via neural networks and Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) algorithms can be mitigated or optimized through several approaches. One method is to replace SGD algorithms with Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) algorithms, which add an exogenous white noise to the gradient descent, providing regularization and allowing the algorithm to escape from local traps. Additionally, using residual connections in the neural network architecture can help propagate gradient information through the many successive layers, although this may not be directly applicable to deep SOC problems due to the fixed structure of the neural network. Another approach is to use local methods in space to estimate the conditional expectation, as seen in the Qknn algorithm, which can provide more accurate results, especially in 1-dimensional control problems. Furthermore, using a Lipschitz version of the driver of the Backward Stochastic Differential Equation (BSDE) can help improve the convergence of the algorithm, as observed in the Y&R algorithm. Overall, these methods can help improve the learning and optimization of SOC problems via neural networks and SGD algorithms, especially in the presence of noise and deep network structures.
context:
Stochastic Optimal Control (SOC), which consists in optimizing a functional of a trajectory of a controlled Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) has applications in a wide range of problems: management of resources, queuing systems, epidemic and population processes, pricing of financial derivatives, portfolio allocation...
In comparison with classic optimal control, SOC models include a random noise with known probability distribution that affects the evolution or the observation of the system. SOC also aims to manage the risk inherent to this noise.SOC problems are usually solved using specific strategies, such as Forward-Backward SDEs (FBSDEs) , or by solving Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) optimality conditions through partial differential equations methods or by stochastic dynamic programming . Such problems can also be solved using Neural Networks calibrated by SGD techniques, .More specifically, in this article we consider the numerical resolution of a SOC problem where the control is parametrized by a neural network calibrated by gradient descent.
This method implies to compute the path-wise derivatives along the trajectory of the SDE of the objective function with respect to the parameters of the neural network, as introduced in , .
Stochastic gradient descent is a very general approach that can be applied to a wide range of problems and which does not need to be specifically adapted to each problem. Moreover, SGD scales very efficiently to high-dimensional problems, contrary to HJB-based methods, and has proved its efficiency on high-dimensional and highly non-convex problems .However, if the neural control is applied at many time points as it is the case for the Euler-Maruyama scheme where the (discrete) control is taken as an approximation of a continuous control, then the SOC problem reads as the optimization of a very deep neural network, which is roughly as deep as the number of times that control can be applied (see Figures REF and REF ).
Very deep neural networks are known to be considerably more difficult to train , and may run into vanishing gradient problems , . Indeed, the deeper the neural network is, the more non-linear it is, thus increasing the number of local traps for the gradient descent such as local (but not global) and saddle points.
In image analysis where very deep convolutional neural networks are commonly used, residual and convolutional dense networks were introduced to deal with this issue. These networks are based on architectures with residual connections to propagate the gradient information through the many successive layers.As it comes to deep SOC, we cannot freely change the structure of the neural network as it is fixed by the equations defining the SOC problem and therefore we cannot directly use residual connections. We can only freely choose the structure of the neural network returning the control, for which a few layers is often enough (see for example , ).A way to improve the learning is to replace SGD algorithms by Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) algorithms. Such optimizers add an exogenous white noise to the gradient descent, providing regularization and allowing to escape from traps. It has indeed been observed that adding noise improves the learning for very deep neural networks, .

input: What are the advantages of using closed-form Wasserstein distance in simplifying VAE loss?
expected_output: The closed-form Wasserstein distance provides a simplified solution for calculating the distance between two distributions, which is beneficial in simplifying the VAE loss. In the case of multivariate Gaussians, the closed-form solution of the Wasserstein distance between two distributions allows for a more straightforward calculation of the Distribution Alignment (DA) loss. Additionally, since the encoder predicts diagonal covariance matrices, which are commutative, the distance simplifies further, making the calculations more efficient. This simplification enables the combination of the basic VAE-loss with cross-alignment and distribution alignment losses, resulting in the Cross- and Distribution Alignment (CADA-VAE) Loss, which can learn shared multimodal embeddings of more than two modalities without requiring examples of all modalities for all classes. Overall, the use of closed-form Wasserstein distance simplifies the VAE loss and enables more efficient calculations, making it a useful tool in variational autoencoder architectures.

input: Does SPECULOOS' detection potential improve with compact low-mass planet systems?
expected_output: The detection potential of SPECULOOS is enhanced in the context of compact low-mass planet systems. This is because the simulations assume that low-mass stars tend to form compact multiple systems of low-mass planets, with each target having at least one planet in a short-period orbit. The probability for a planet to exist in a given period range is fixed to 50%, and increases to 80% if a planet is already present in a shorter orbit, which favors the detection of planets in compact systems. Additionally, the assumption of nearly coplanar systems allows for a higher likelihood of transit events, further improving the detection potential of SPECULOOS for such systems.
context: We performed Monte-Carlo simulations to estimate the detection potential of SPECULOOS. Each simulation looped within the current SPECULOOS target list (1136 UCDs with {{formula:b28ddbde-42d5-4a44-8eb6-5316f01c16eb}} -mag {{formula:af2e9696-6777-467a-a83a-bacb91975106}} 12.5). For each target, a value for the mass, radius, and effective temperature was drawn from the normal distributions shown in Table REF , and a typical observation window was drawn, assuming {{formula:a4521dc5-51e6-4331-b1d6-cf81b91ef7e8}} nights of observation in total - {{formula:2a39432a-f582-4f05-ad28-a25cea1dada1}} depending on the spectral type (see Section REF ) - and a continuous observation sequence of 8 hours per night. A planetary system was then drawn for the star, based on the structure of the TRAPPIST-1 system. The orbital periods were divided in 8 possible bins: 1-2 d, 2-3.5 d, 3.5-5.5 d, 5.5-8 d, 8-11 d, 11-14.5 d, 14.5-18.5 d, and 18.5-23 d. For each period range, the probability for a planet to exist was fixed to 50%, and 80% if a planet was already present in a shorter orbit, assuming thus that low-mass stars tend to form compact multiple systems of low-mass planets and that each of our targets has at least one planet in a short-period orbit. An orbital period was attributed to each planet assuming a uniform probability distribution within its given period range. The orbits were assumed to be circular, and semi-major axes were computed using Kepler's third law. The mass and radius of each planet were drawn from the normal distributions shown in Table REF , based on the mean and standard deviations of the masses and radii of the seven TRAPPIST-1 planets . A value for the cosine of the orbital inclination {{formula:70515ac6-79e9-4a3d-8d9b-43f1c734335e}} of the inner planet of the system was drawn from the uniform distribution {{formula:7a9f20ef-ed8a-4368-a36a-7195e31175f3}} . Then inclinations were drawn for the outer planets from the normal distribution {{formula:b7ef6bc2-edb5-4719-bf0e-440216a2ec6d}} , assuming thus a nearly coplanar system.For each planet, the impact parameter at inferior conjunction was computed. If smaller than 1, the depth and duration of the transit were computed, a random phase was drawn for the orbit, and the code checked if a transit happened within the observation window. If a transit was observed, a photometric signal-to-noise was computed based on its duration and on the expected photometric precision of a SPECULOOS 1m telescope for the star, given its spectral type and magnitude, as computed using the SPECULOOS-South Observatory Exposure Time Calculator. A noise floor level of 500 ppm was assumed to represent the red noises of instrumental, atmospheric, and astrophysical origins. At the end, if the resulting signal-to-noise was larger than 5, the transit was assumed to be detected, and the parameters of the planet and the star registered.We performed 1000 simulations that resulted for the detected planets in the probability distributions shown in Figure REF . Planets with irradiations between 25 and 150% times the one of the Earth were assumed to be temperate.

input: How does infinite axiology differ in total vs average utilitarianism?
expected_output: Infinite axiology differs in total vs average utilitarianism in that total utilitarianism can be extended to infinite contexts by comparing the sum of differences in welfare between two populations, whereas average utilitarianism is less clear in its extension to infinite contexts. However, a possible approach for average utilitarianism is to use the limiting relative frequency of welfare levels in an infinite population, allowing for the calculation of average welfare. In the context of infinite worlds, average utilitarians may compare outcomes by using an infinite generalization of critical-level utilitarianism, where the critical level is the average welfare level in the background population. This suggests that average utilitarianism may agree with its additive counterpart, total utilitarianism, in the infinite context, but this requires a well-defined notion of relative frequency for infinite worlds.
context: A long-standing and unresolved challenge for axiology is how to extend axiologies from finite to infinite contexts.For surveys of the difficulties of infinite axiology, see for instance, and Ch. 1 of . Most of the extant proposals for ranking infinite worlds, in both philosophy and economics, aim to extend total utilitarianism.See, for instance, (forthcoming), and (ms), among many others. However, these proposals can easily be adapted to extend other additive axiologies. For instance, a simple extension of total utilitarianism (suggested in ) simply compares any two populations by summing the differences in welfare between the two populations for each individual, treating an individual who doesn't exist in a population as having welfare 0.Formally, {{formula:2ba4290f-6c96-47d5-b199-d1661ac9a636}} if and only if {{formula:05b39fa2-f6f8-4968-a4c7-45e5284e02ed}} converges unconditionally to a value {{formula:c4621236-dedf-431d-ad68-220fdef4a1ca}} , where for any {{formula:e27d5584-b65d-496b-9f27-16fc95912655}} , {{formula:a7c79cdf-053b-4699-a93f-10c7315b1a71}} (and likewise for {{formula:c4aa8cf2-63d8-491f-b761-30115a1d58c1}} ). This axiological criterion can easily be adapted to a critical-level or prioritarian theory by simply replacing welfare with some increasing function of welfare.It is much less clear, however, how to extend non-additive theories to the infinite context, and there has so far been little if any discussion of this question. Our limit results, however, suggest a partial answer: when comparing two infinite populations, at least when these populations differ only finitely, we are quite literally in (and not merely approaching) the large-background-population limit. So it is natural to think that a non-additive axiology {{formula:775cfdb9-de30-4f10-94ec-735a9ddf867a}} that has an additive counterpart {{formula:fa261504-3a6d-4ff7-a734-a1cdbe700cab}} should agree exactly with that additive counterpart in the infinite context. For instance, if we are average utilitarians and we live in an infinite world, but we can only affect a finite part of that infinite world, then we should simply compare the possible outcomes of our choices by the appropriate infinite generalization of critical-level utilitarianism, where the critical level is the average welfare level in the background population.This suggestion is well-defined only if we have a well-defined notion of relative frequency for infinite worlds—specifically, the relative frequency of different welfare levels in an infinite population, which lets us make sense of further notions like a welfare distribution and average welfare. A natural suggestion here (advocated, for instance, by ) is to use the limiting relative frequency in uniformly expanding spatiotemporal regions, providing that this limit exists and is the same for all starting locations. There is plenty of debate to be had about this proposal, but this is not the place for that debate. At any rate, it seems plausible (though far from indisputable) that there should be some way of making sense of the relative frequencies of particular welfare levels in an infinite population.

The doomsday argument has practical applications. If you care about
the future of the human race you might want to reduce the probability
of possible causes of extinction that you might have some control
over. The degree to which you should be concerned with such possible
causes depends on how likely they are, and if you accept the doomsday
argument you should think the possible dooms more likely than you
would otherwise have thought.The argument presented here should change your calculation. You
should not think a process is more likely if it affects us alone, but
you should think it more likely if it affects civilizations everywhere
in the universe. To continue the above example, you should be more
concerned that a large number of asteroids have not yet been detected
than about the particular orbit of each one. You should not worry
especially about the chance that some specific nearby star will become
a supernova, but more about the chance that supernovas are more deadly
to nearby life than we believe. Many other examples are possible.

input: What is the process for using CH to model shallow water waves effectively?
expected_output: The Camassa-Holm (CH) equation is used to model shallow water waves by first deducing the equation as a model for shallow water waves, and then showing that it is an integrable equation admitting a bi-Hamiltonian formulation and a Lax pair. The equation is then solved to obtain continuous peaked wave solutions that collide without changing their shapes and speeds. To use the CH equation effectively, researchers have also sought further generalizations or correlated equations that would share some or the same properties, such as the Dullin-Gottwald-Holm (DGH) equation. Additionally, the well-posedness of the CH equation in Sobolev and similar spaces has been studied, and local well-posedness has been determined for initial data in certain spaces. The CH equation has also been shown to have a critical value, below which the equation is not locally well-posed, and the uniform continuity of solutions does not hold. Overall, the process for using the CH equation to model shallow water waves effectively involves understanding the mathematical and physical properties of the equation and its solutions, as well as the limitations and challenges of working with the equation.

input: Does adding appearance descriptors to gaze zone estimation actually enhance its performance compared to traditional methods?
expected_output: According to the context, adding appearance descriptors to gaze zone estimation does enhance its performance compared to traditional methods. The work presented in the paper introduces an appearance descriptor as an additional feature to augment the state of the eyes, which allows for an increased number of gaze zones without compromising performance. This is evident from the evaluation on a dataset composed of multiple drivers, which shows that the inclusion of appearance descriptors does not come at the expense of performance. In contrast, traditional methods, such as the work by Fridman et al., have limitations, including overfitting to user-based models and failing to generalize well with global-based models, due to the design of their features. Therefore, the addition of appearance descriptors is a beneficial enhancement to gaze zone estimation.
context:
In literature, works on gaze zone estimation are relatively new and of those,
there are two categories: geometric and learning based methods.
The work presented in estimates gaze zones
based on geometric methods, where a 3-D model car is divided into different zones
and 3D gaze tracking is used to classify gaze into predefined zones; however, no
evaluations on gaze zone level is given. Another
geometric based method is presented in , but the number of
gaze zones estimated is very limited (i.e. on-road versus off-road) and
evaluations are conducted in stationary vehicles. In terms of learning based
methods, there are two prevalent works. Work by Tawari et al.
 has the most similarity to the work presented in this
paper in terms of the features selected (e.g. head pose, horizontal gaze surrogate),
classifier used (i.e. random forest)
and evaluation on naturalistic driving data. The difference is that this work
introduces another feature to augment the state of the eyes (i.e. appearance
descriptor), which allows for an increased number of gaze zones, but not at the
expense of performance, as shown by evaluating on a dataset composed of multiple drivers.
Another learning based method is the work presented by Fridman
et al. where the evaluations are done on
a significantly large dataset, but the design of the features to represent
the state of the head and eyes are what is causing their classifier to over fit
to user based models and to not generalize well with global based models.

The environment inside the car is relatively controlled in that the camera position is fixed and the driver torso moves
in a fairly contained space. Thus, a camera can be positioned such that the driver's face is always fully or almost
fully in the field of view. However, the lighting conditions are sometimes drastically variable (e.g. quickly passing
under a bridge, reflection of the sun on the camera lens, etc.) and thus there are frequently cases where the intensity
distribution of the image does not allow for successful detection of the face (i.e. false reject). Every detection step
in the pipeline is tuned to have a low False Accept Rate (FAR). A false accept error early in the pipeline propagates
and can result in drastically incorrect head pose and eye pose estimation. In the context of video-based driver gaze
classification, a high False Reject Rate (FRR) is more acceptable than a high FAR.The face detector in our pipeline uses a Histogram of Oriented Gradients (HOG) combined with a linear SVM classifier, an
image pyramid, and sliding window detection scheme implemented in the DLIB C++ library . The performance of
this detector has lower FAR than the widely-used default Haar-feature-based face detector available in OpenCV
 and thus is more appropriate for our application.

input: What causes vanishing gradients in deep neural networks for Stochastic Optimal Control?
expected_output: The vanishing gradients in deep neural networks for Stochastic Optimal Control are caused by the increasing non-linearity of the network as it becomes deeper, which leads to a higher number of local traps for the gradient descent, such as local but not global minima and saddle points. This issue arises because the deeper the neural network is, the more difficult it is to train, and the gradients used to update the parameters during backpropagation become smaller, making it harder for the network to learn and converge. Additionally, when the neural control is applied at many time points, as in the Euler-Maruyama scheme, the Stochastic Optimal Control problem becomes equivalent to optimizing a very deep neural network, which exacerbates the vanishing gradient problem.
context:
Stochastic Optimal Control (SOC), which consists in optimizing a functional of a trajectory of a controlled Stochastic Differential Equation (SDE) has applications in a wide range of problems: management of resources, queuing systems, epidemic and population processes, pricing of financial derivatives, portfolio allocation...
In comparison with classic optimal control, SOC models include a random noise with known probability distribution that affects the evolution or the observation of the system. SOC also aims to manage the risk inherent to this noise.SOC problems are usually solved using specific strategies, such as Forward-Backward SDEs (FBSDEs) , or by solving Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) optimality conditions through partial differential equations methods or by stochastic dynamic programming . Such problems can also be solved using Neural Networks calibrated by SGD techniques, .More specifically, in this article we consider the numerical resolution of a SOC problem where the control is parametrized by a neural network calibrated by gradient descent.
This method implies to compute the path-wise derivatives along the trajectory of the SDE of the objective function with respect to the parameters of the neural network, as introduced in , .
Stochastic gradient descent is a very general approach that can be applied to a wide range of problems and which does not need to be specifically adapted to each problem. Moreover, SGD scales very efficiently to high-dimensional problems, contrary to HJB-based methods, and has proved its efficiency on high-dimensional and highly non-convex problems .However, if the neural control is applied at many time points as it is the case for the Euler-Maruyama scheme where the (discrete) control is taken as an approximation of a continuous control, then the SOC problem reads as the optimization of a very deep neural network, which is roughly as deep as the number of times that control can be applied (see Figures REF and REF ).
Very deep neural networks are known to be considerably more difficult to train , and may run into vanishing gradient problems , . Indeed, the deeper the neural network is, the more non-linear it is, thus increasing the number of local traps for the gradient descent such as local (but not global) and saddle points.
In image analysis where very deep convolutional neural networks are commonly used, residual and convolutional dense networks were introduced to deal with this issue. These networks are based on architectures with residual connections to propagate the gradient information through the many successive layers.As it comes to deep SOC, we cannot freely change the structure of the neural network as it is fixed by the equations defining the SOC problem and therefore we cannot directly use residual connections. We can only freely choose the structure of the neural network returning the control, for which a few layers is often enough (see for example , ).A way to improve the learning is to replace SGD algorithms by Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics (SGLD) algorithms. Such optimizers add an exogenous white noise to the gradient descent, providing regularization and allowing to escape from traps. It has indeed been observed that adding noise improves the learning for very deep neural networks, .

By design, DenseNets allow layers access to feature-maps from all of its preceding layers (although sometimes through transition layers). We conduct an experiment to investigate if a trained network takes advantage of this opportunity.
We first train a DenseNet on C10+ with {{formula:59e56f19-d237-4c4b-b47d-ff86cac006e6}} and {{formula:39c3444b-b638-4283-a637-08d9f0844b68}} . For each convolutional layer {{formula:06b0e30c-5ed4-42d9-891a-59f167d127ad}} within a block, we compute the average (absolute) weight assigned to connections with layer {{formula:c212663d-8ee1-443b-8c79-3146b2bf8e13}} . Figure REF shows a heat-map for all three dense blocks.
The average absolute weight serves as a surrogate for the dependency of a convolutional layer on its preceding layers.
A red dot in position ({{formula:ffc42ee2-2821-40b1-ba19-8f4d007bca9a}} ) indicates that the layer {{formula:d9d29f3b-31f9-4c90-897d-e9910d802467}} makes, on average, strong use of feature-maps produced {{formula:7b5c82b6-feed-4eb5-a290-2e4c71950d16}} -layers before.
Several observations can be made from the plot:All layers spread their weights over many inputs within the same block. This indicates that features extracted by very early layers are, indeed, directly used by deep layers throughout the same dense block.

The weights of the transition layers also spread their weight across all layers within the preceding dense block, indicating information flow from the first to the last layers of the DenseNet through few indirections.

The layers within the second and third dense block consistently assign the least weight to the outputs of the transition layer (the top row of the triangles), indicating that the transition layer outputs many redundant features (with low weight on average). This is in keeping with the strong results of DenseNet-BC where exactly these outputs are compressed.

Although the final classification layer, shown on the very right, also uses weights across the entire dense block, there seems to be a concentration towards final feature-maps, suggesting that there may be some more high-level features produced late in the network.

[Figure: The average absolute filter weights of convolutional layers in a trained DenseNet. The color of pixel (s,ℓ)(s,\ell ) encodes the average L1L1 norm (normalized by number of input feature-maps) of the weights connecting convolutional layer ss to ℓ\ell within a dense block. Three columns highlighted by black rectangles correspond to two transition layers and the classification layer. The first row encodes weights connected to the input layer of the dense block.]

expected_output: Immunotherapy impacts tumor growth via lymphocyte dynamics by introducing a periodic function that models the effect of immunotherapy, which can lead to a decrease in the "input rate" of lymphocytes. The model shows that for effective values of doses and frequencies higher than certain thresholds, the system can revert from uncontrolled growth to a treatment-controlled population. However, the model also reveals a "paradoxical" phenomenon where the enhancement of the immune system with immunotherapy can stimulate tumor growth at given frequencies above those localized in the region of controllable growth of malignant cells. The impact of immunotherapy on tumor growth is highly dependent on the immunological response of each individual, the malignant cells population at the beginning of the treatment, and the rate of proliferation of the tissue.

input: How does the MW approach compare to the classical approach in achieving Nash equilibria?
expected_output: The MW approach does not make determining Nash equilibria more difficult than the classical approach, as the dimension of the output game is always equal to the input game. In fact, determining Nash equilibria or evolutionarily stable strategies have the same level of difficulty in both the classical and quantum games, according to the MW scheme. This suggests that the MW approach does not introduce additional complexity in achieving Nash equilibria compared to the classical approach.

input: How can the architecture, loss function, and optimizer of a CNN be optimized for effective image classification in DR datasets?
expected_output: The architecture of a CNN can be optimized for effective image classification in DR datasets by utilizing different architectures, such as ResNet34 and VGG16, and varying the image data resolution, training set selection, number of training epochs, and data augmentation strengths. The binary-crossentropy loss function and the Adam optimizer can be used during training, with all network parameters initialized with the weights from pre-trained models. Additionally, training the models with non-incipient disease data first and then continuing to train with all training data can help reduce the total training effort and improve model performance. The use of ensemble methods, where multiple models are combined, can also improve the overall performance of the CNN. Furthermore, fine-tuning the models on the object detection data and using techniques such as "Networks on Conv feature maps" (NoC) and region proposal network (RPN) can also enhance the image classification capabilities of the CNN.
context: We used CNN models for classifying image models in the DR dataset. The CNN models were implemented using pytorch . The deep learning models used to construct our ensembles vary in their architecture, image data resolution, training set selection, number of training epochs and data augmentation strengths. Two different CNN architectures, ResNet34  and VGG16 , were used in our experiments. We used the binary-crossentropy loss function and the Adam  optimizer during training. All network parameters were initialized with the weights from pretrained models provided by the torchvision  package that were created for classifying objects from the ImageNet database.Since our experiments involved scanning various {{formula:4d91782e-900c-43d9-bf6e-9d9b4f5df8d5}} values, to reduce the total training effort, we first trained our models with non-incipient disease data (only SL0 & SL3 & SL4) for 130 epochs, and then continued to train the resulting networks with all training data (SL0 to SL4) till convergence. Most trained models reached an AUC of above {{formula:4a0308df-9211-4141-93de-c168f2b2b0fe}} on both the training and the validation sets. We discarded the bad performing models and put the rest into a pool. The retained models in the pool were then used as base learners for constructing ensembles. To create an ensemble model instance, we randomly picked {{formula:78478ad2-2a0b-4ae0-8491-992c1f74dcc8}} single learners from the pool. In our experiment, we evaluated {{formula:e912997b-2223-475e-8be4-20d229ec2f87}} and {{formula:9ec9ffd0-e069-4493-8bf7-86328a935c3c}} , two ensemble sizes used in previous works , . Their individual predictions were then combined and grouped for later analysis.

In this section we introduce our detection method based on the baseline Faster R-CNN system.
The models are initialized by the ImageNet classification models, and then fine-tuned on the object detection data. We have experimented with ResNet-50/101 at the time of the ILSVRC & COCO 2015 detection competitions.Unlike VGG-16 used in , our ResNet has no hidden fc layers. We adopt the idea of “Networks on Conv feature maps” (NoC) to address this issue.
We compute the full-image shared conv feature maps using those layers whose strides on the image are no greater than 16 pixels (, conv1, conv2_ x, conv3_x, and conv4_x, totally 91 conv layers in ResNet-101; Table REF ). We consider these layers as analogous to the 13 conv layers in VGG-16, and by doing so, both ResNet and VGG-16 have conv feature maps of the same total stride (16 pixels).
These layers are shared by a region proposal network (RPN, generating 300 proposals) and a Fast R-CNN detection network .
RoI pooling is performed before conv5_1. On this RoI-pooled feature, all layers of conv5_x and up are adopted for each region, playing the roles of VGG-16's fc layers.
The final classification layer is replaced by two sibling layers (classification and box regression ).For the usage of BN layers, after pre-training, we compute the BN statistics (means and variances) for each layer on the ImageNet training set. Then the BN layers are fixed during fine-tuning for object detection. As such, the BN layers become linear activations with constant offsets and scales, and BN statistics are not updated by fine-tuning. We fix the BN layers mainly for reducing memory consumption in Faster R-CNN training.PASCAL VOCFollowing, for the PASCAL VOC 2007 test set, we use the 5k trainval images in VOC 2007 and 16k trainval images in VOC 2012 for training (“07+12”). For the PASCAL VOC 2012 test set, we use the 10k trainval+test images in VOC 2007 and 16k trainval images in VOC 2012 for training (“07++12”). The hyper-parameters for training Faster R-CNN are the same as in .
Table REF shows the results. ResNet-101 improves the mAP by {{formula:3ab3c272-94c0-40bf-bb84-01c4323bca15}} 3% over VGG-16. This gain is solely because of the improved features learned by ResNet.MS COCOThe MS COCO dataset involves 80 object categories. We evaluate the PASCAL VOC metric (mAP @ IoU = 0.5) and the standard COCO metric (mAP @ IoU = .5:.05:.95). We use the 80k images on the train set for training and the 40k images on the val set for evaluation.
Our detection system for COCO is similar to that for PASCAL VOC.
We train the COCO models with an 8-GPU implementation, and thus the RPN step has a mini-batch size of 8 images (, 1 per GPU) and the Fast R-CNN step has a mini-batch size of 16 images. The RPN step and Fast R-CNN step are both trained for 240k iterations with a learning rate of 0.001 and then for 80k iterations with 0.0001.Table REF shows the results on the MS COCO validation set. ResNet-101 has a 6% increase of mAP@[.5, .95] over VGG-16, which is a 28% relative improvement, solely contributed by the features learned by the better network.

input: Does MF interaction actually enhance the MFG-SB link, and if so, what are the key mechanisms by which this enhancement occurs?
expected_output: The introduction of MF interaction does indeed enhance the link between the Mean Field Game (MFG) and the Schrödinger Bridge (SB) frameworks. This enhancement occurs through the generalization of the PDEs in the MFG framework, which incorporates the MF interaction term, thereby establishing a deeper connection to optimal transport and the SB framework. The key mechanisms by which this enhancement occurs include the application of the Hopf-Cole transform, which yields a system of PDEs that can be related to the SB framework, and the design of variational recursions that solve the Schrödinger Bridge Problem (SBP) with gradient or mixed conservative-dissipative drift. Additionally, the introduction of Lyapunov functionals, or "free energy functionals", allows for the recasting of the FPK PDEs as a gradient flow on the manifold of probability density functions, which facilitates the development of grid-less recursive algorithms for solving the FPK PDE. Overall, the incorporation of MF interaction provides a more comprehensive and nuanced understanding of the relationship between the MFG and SB frameworks.

This correspondence allows for the calculation of the central charge of the O(n) model, which agrees with other methods of calculation and lends support to the interpretation of the stress tensor for curves satisfying conformal restriction. Additionally, the use of twist operators in the Simmons-Cardy construction of the probabilities for the SLE trace to wind in various ways about marked points also plays a crucial role in understanding the connection between the stress tensor and central charge interpretation. The calculation of the scaling dimension of twist operators and the partition function for the loop model in presence of twist operators further supports this connection.

input: What is the statistical structure of stationary points and how does it influence energy landscape complexity?
expected_output: The statistical structure of stationary points, including minima, maxima, and saddles, plays a crucial role in understanding the complexity of energy landscapes. Research has shown that a sharp transition occurs from a simple landscape with typically only a single stationary point to a complex, glassy landscape with exponentially many stationary points as certain parameters are varied. This transition is characterized by a change in the mean number of stationary points and the nature of the Hessian matrix, which describes the stability of local equilibria. A gapped or gapless spectrum of the Hessian matrix at low-lying local minima is a key feature that influences the energy landscape complexity, with a gapless spectrum indicating the existence of very flat directions in configuration space. The statistical structure of stationary points has significant implications for various fields, including theoretical physics, statistical physics, neural networks, and complex dynamics, and is an active area of research in both pure and applied mathematics.

input: How can deep learning frameworks be used to assess muscle activation via SoS inversion?
expected_output: Deep learning frameworks can be used to assess muscle activation via SoS inversion by training a neural network to take raw US channel data as input and produce sound speed maps as output. This is achieved by training the network using simulation data, where the network learns to extract cues regarding the sound speed of the domain through which the US pulse has propagated, which are hidden in the measured signal. The trained network can then be applied to pre-beamformed raw RF channel data to generate sound speed maps, allowing for the assessment of muscle activation and functional muscle imaging. The structure of the network, including the combination of inputs at different layers, can affect the reconstruction results and stability to noise, with some configurations showing improvement in reconstruction results.
context:
It also depends on the bulk modulus, which is expected to increase during muscle contraction as well.In this work, we explore the feasibility of SoS inversion to the application of assessing muscle activation and functional muscle imaging based on modifications to a previously presented deep learning framework for sound speed inversion . The SoS inversion network is applied to the pre-beamformed raw RF channel data generated from a single acoustic plane wave (Fig. REF ). Cues regarding the sound speed of the domain through which the US pulse has propagated are hidden in the measured signal. However, most of this information is discarded as part of the classic delay and sum and envelope detection steps of the b-mode imaging process.
[Figure: B-Mode image of the calf muscles (a), the soleus and gastorcnemius. We opt to work with raw US channel data (b - cropped) instead as most cues required for SoS inversion are discarded as part of the image formation step.]Deep learning has seen increasing popularity and success in the fields of vision and medical imaging for such tasks as classification, detection, and segmentation. However, only recently, deep learning has started being applied to physics and inverse problems and the imaging pipeline , . A neural network can be viewed as a black box performing non-linear regression with a set of parameters that control the relationship of the output on the input. The structure of the network affects both training properties as well as regularization, through the expressibility of the network. In this case, we wish to train the network to take raw channel data as input and produce sound speed maps as output. This is done by training it using simulation data.

While combining multiple inputs at the first layer (“Start Network”) does not improve reconstruction results, combining in both the middle (“Middle Network”) and the end (“End Network”) does provide some improvement, as can be seen, Table REF and Figure REF . input: Can resolvable designs actually enhance the flexibility of Feature Request (FR) code?
expected_output: Yes, resolvable designs can actually enhance the flexibility of Fractional Repetition (FR) codes. The resolvable nature of the codes allows for a natural tradeoff between the repetition degree and the number of parallel classes, enabling the construction of FR codes with higher or lower repetition degrees simply by including or removing parallel classes. This flexibility is lacking in existing approaches that rely on entire Steiner systems, which may not be resolvable. The use of resolvable designs, such as affine geometries and Hadamard designs, provides a larger family of codes with varying repetition degrees, addressing an open question in previous work.
context:

In contrast, our constructions based on affine geometries and Hadamard designs (cf. Section ), allow for a large family of codes where {{formula:25b7610d-2961-406d-bab8-c8a2dd54a28f}} .

The resolvable nature of our codes allows for a natural tradeoff between the repetition degree {{formula:9f685ca1-5f8d-440a-904b-7b1b3cc42858}} and the number of parallel classes, i.e., we can obtain FR codes with higher or lower {{formula:65166412-f21a-4fc3-a7ba-a5ea42ab9132}} simply by including or removing parallel classes. This flexibility is lacking in the approach of , where the entire Steiner system needs to be used. In particular, it is known that there exist Steiner systems that are not resolvable. For instance, Ray-Chaudhuri and Wilson showed that a resolvable {{formula:f4894f33-4418-47e2-930b-2eda815369ec}} exists if and only if {{formula:7465c66c-5588-44c5-bdab-545e02fa5368}} ().
